nytimes.com.title: Too Many Chips in One Basket?
nytimes.com.text:
A week ago, we learned the news that Jensen Huang, the rock star C.E.O. of the chip-making company Nvidia, had acknowledged an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. It turns out that may have been just the beginning. Shortly after revelations of a second affair, this time with a subordinate, Huang resigned.
Nvidia’s stock has tumbled in the days since, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in value, and analysts have begun trying to process just how the downfall of one of the most important figures in the A.I. industry is going to play out. One Silicon Valley venture capitalist recently called him “irreplaceable.”
But why are Huang and Nvidia so irreplaceable — and is anything that cannot be replaced automatically vulnerable? Today I’m writing about power, vulnerability and choke points.
Why there’s only one Nvidia
Last week, as it became clear that Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia might be in jeopardy, a meme began making the rounds on the internet. It showed a complicated, multitiered structure, delicately balanced on a tiny block. The structure was labeled “entire global economy”; the block was labeled “Jensen Huang’s wife.”
The meme is already outdated: Huang has resigned from his role as Nvidia’s C.E.O. (and it never made sense to put any of this on his wife). But the image still captured the idea that so much of the business world somehow came to depend on one man and his — now, it seems, questionable — judgment.

nytimes.com.title: A Year On, Canada’s Mark Carney Returns to China a Political Star
nytimes.com.text:
The importance of Europe to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify Canada’s economy and politics away from its reliance on the United States was underscored last week by his travel schedule.
Mr. Carney added a stop in Dublin, joining a meeting of European leaders before the start of a previously planned trip to Asia.
Last month Mr. Carney announced that Canada is officially seeking to become the first “associate member” of the European Union. But experts say that Asia offers the greater economic opportunity.
“Prime Minister Carney certainly seems to have a strong focus on Europe, which gives an impression that he is not looking toward Asia,” said Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s graduate school of public policy. “Nevertheless, if Canada is to avoid dependence on the U.S. market and form a coalition of middle powers, cooperation with Asia is essential.”
Last year, Mr. Carney was something of a curiosity at the meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. But his speech in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, and President Trump’s addition of energy security threats to his trade war with the world have made Mr. Carney and his energy-rich country a marquee attraction at both.

nytimes.com.title: Searching for the Last Stoats of Waiheke Island
nytimes.com.text:
To catch a stoat, you need to think like one. For Tilde Sorensen, that means imagining having tiny legs and picturing which route the weasel-like creature might take as it haunts the wilderness of New Zealand, preying on unique birdlife.
Then she sets up a trap along that path.
“We’ve caught all of the ones that will happily go into a trap. So now we’ve got to figure out how to get the really shy ones,” Ms. Sorensen said of the stoat population on Waiheke Island, a 40-minute boat ride from New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland.
“We’re trying to work ourselves out of a job.”
Ms. Sorensen is a stoat-detect-and-respond coordinator for a project called Te Korowai o Waiheke, a Māori name that means The Cloak of Waiheke. It has captured more than 280 stoats since 2020 and, while it is not known how many remain, testing suggests the population has dwindled.
The campaign to eradicate stoats, and many other introduced species, has widespread support in New Zealand, where introduced predators, including rats and possums, kill about 25 million native birds each year.
Waiheke Island, which covers about 36 square miles, is home to 4,300 people, a number that swells to about 45,000 in the summer.

nytimes.com.title: They Defeated a Strongman. But Can They Run a Country?
nytimes.com.text:
They had no leader, no political party and no conventional campaign. They made decisions by raising their hands after hours of debate in university classrooms, a slow and cumbersome process billed as a unique experiment in direct democracy.
That free-form approach to politics of Serbia’s students proved so effective that, in a general election on Oct. 25, they achieved what established opposition parties had failed to accomplish for more than a decade: routing the well-oiled political machine of Serbia’s strongman leader, Aleksandar Vucic.
Mr. Vucic, nearing the end of his second term as president and barred from running again, had resigned as president a month before the October vote for a new Parliament, gambling that his governing party would win and that he could keep his grip on power by becoming prime minister. He had held that post twice before.
His plan was upended by the election victory of a slate of parliamentary candidates selected by students in freewheeling campus meetings. Their selections and electoral successes marked the culmination of a striking exercise in collective decision making. That approach, some believe, could hold lessons for democratic movements beyond Serbia.
But the principles that carried the students to victory may not, on their own, be enough to build a functioning, coherent and durable government.
The diverse list of candidates chosen by the students, nearly all political novices with a wide range of sometimes contradictory views, reflected a belief that everyone should have a say in a leaderless movement united by the single objective of getting rid of Mr. Vucic and the system he created.

nytimes.com.title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, Mexican Drug Lord, Dies in Prison
nytimes.com.text:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a notorious Mexican drug lord who helped build the foundations of the modern drug trade, died a prisoner at the age of 80 on Sunday, according to the Mexican authorities.
Mr. Félix Gallardo became internationally known in the 1980s after the United States Drug Enforcement Administration accused him of the kidnapping, torture and murder of an undercover agent, Enrique (Kiki) Salazar Camarena.
On Friday, after decades behind bars, Mr. Félix Gallardo was transferred from the Puente Grande prison complex to a private hospital in Guadalajara after a medical emergency, according to the Jalisco state secretary of public security. He died around 2 p.m. Sunday of multiple organ failure, the agency said in a statement, citing medical personnel who treated him.
A small religious ceremony will be held at the hospital in the presence of his relatives, according to Jorge Eduardo Montiel, a spokesman for the Secretary of Public Security of Jalisco state.
When Mr. Félix Gallardo was arrested in 1989, he was described by the Mexican attorney general, Enrique Alvarez del Castillo, as the “No. 1 narcotics trafficker in Mexico.”

nytimes.com.title: Trump’s Oil Grab in Venezuela Is Testing the Country’s National Identity
nytimes.com.text:
Like generations before him, Leonardo Silva grew up steeped in beliefs about the extraordinarily abundant resource that made Venezuela special. All the oil under their feet was theirs, they felt. Virtually free gasoline was a birthright. To be born atop this bounty was like winning the lottery.
Mr. Silva, 38, said his generation viewed oil as a cornerstone of the country’s national identity, when a booming economy allowed Venezuela to occupy a privileged tier in the global order. His children, he said, have a far less rosy view.
“To them oil isn’t important, it’s secondary,” said Mr. Silva, who works at a foundation in Caracas helping people with disabilities. “They don’t have that culture of us being a rich country. They just know that if you don’t work, you don’t eat.”
Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent that is rare outside the Middle East for more than a century, becoming a defining feature of the social fabric like baseball, beauty pageants or the veneration of the liberation hero Simón Bolívar.
But now the U.S. government is taking control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil. And, pressed by economic need, long-held nationalist convictions about oil, starting with the need for sovereign control, are giving way to a more complex web of perspectives.
The ways in which Venezuelans are re-evaluating oil, and by extension their reliance on it, are the result of immense upheaval over the last decade. Oil production plummeted because of mismanagement, political purges, corruption and sanctions.

nytimes.com.title: Jordan Sentences 3 to Death Over Greek Orthodox Church Attack
nytimes.com.text:
A military-run court in Jordan sentenced three men to death on Sunday after they were convicted in connection with an attack at a church last month that killed nine people, the Jordanian Armed Forces said in a statement.
The shooting at a Greek Orthodox church, which also wounded about three dozen people, was one of the deadliest militant attacks in the country in years, and King Abdullah II vowed that it would be met with “the harshest retaliation.”
The three men were sentenced after being convicted of violating antiterrorism laws, according to the Jordanian military. They were found guilty of carrying out deadly terrorist acts, possessing weapons and ammunition with the intent to commit terrorism, and promoting the ideas of a terrorist group.
That group was not named in the armed forces statement.
The sentences are subject to appeal, the military statement noted.
The three men were arrested in late October in Jordan after a shootout with security forces during a predawn raid on their hide-out in an abandoned house in the southern province of Karak, where the church attack took place. Karak is home to a sizable Christian community.
King Abdullah praised the arrests on social media. “No proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he wrote.
Jordanian officials have not said what motivated the shooting at the church. Shortly afterward, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said it was “the result of terrorist takfiri ideology,” using an Arabic phrase that often describes Islamist extremists who declare other Muslims heretics.
The sentencing on Sunday came a weeks after Jordan retaliated for the church attack with deadly airstrikes on Islamic State targets in southern Syria, a Jordanian government spokesman said at the time. The Jordanian military said it had been “targeting hide-outs of terrorist organizations,” without naming any specific group.
The airstrikes in Syria killed at least seven civilians, including three children, according to the Syrian civil defense rescue service, and the attack was condemned by Syrian officials.
Muslims make up more than 97 percent of the population in Jordan, and Christians make up about 2 percent, according to United States government estimates. The country’s Constitution declares Islam the state religion but safeguards the free exercise of religion and bars discrimination on religious grounds. Christian Jordanians are guaranteed seats in Parliament and have long served as cabinet ministers and ambassadors.
The Christian presence in Karak dates back more than 1,500 years, and there are multiple churches there to this day. Jordan also has important biblical and Christian pilgrimage sites, including one along the Jordan River where Jesus was said to have been baptized.
In June, Jordan hanged six men convicted of terrorism-related or drug-trafficking charges. The executions came after a nine-year hiatus in executions and were condemned by the European Union and human rights groups, including the Death Penalty Information Center and Human Rights Watch.
Raja Abdulrahim contributed reporting.

nytimes.com.title: Saudi-Backed Forces Retreat in Yemen, Leaving Key Strait in Houthi Control
nytimes.com.text:
Forces backed by Saudi Arabia in Yemen said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from the country’s Red Sea coast, where they have been fighting for weeks to retake strategic territory from the Iran-aligned Houthi militia.
A group of fighters called the Southern Armed Forces, who are allied with the government of Yemen, said in a statement that they were “redeploying” to protect the interim capital, Aden, citing recent battlefield developments and “threats targeting” the city.
Aden has been the seat of the internationally recognized government for more than a decade, since the Houthis seized control of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital.
The retreat is a blow for the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia as the balance of power in Yemen continues to tilt toward the Houthis, analysts said.
“The Houthis are very determined to go to Aden,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group. “They don’t want to see any area controlled by the government or the Saudi side, so they want to take over everything at this moment.”

nytimes.com.title: Israel Kidnapped Iranian Generals in Hunt for Ron Arad
nytimes.com.text:
Gen. Abdullah Saberi, an Iranian commander, stepped out for a jog early one morning in an upscale diplomatic quarter of Syria’s capital. Israeli intelligence officers waited nearby. Posing as movers, they had slipped past the neighborhood’s security checkpoints.
As he headed for a nearby park, General Saberi passed two men who carried an oversize refrigerator box. In a flash, the men restrained the general, drugged him, threw the box over his head, shoved him into a white van and left as if nothing had happened.
He was whisked to Israel for interrogation, according to numerous officials in the Middle East, including senior Iranian officials close to General Saberi and a Syrian official who reviewed video of the September 2021 kidnapping.
As a veteran of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, General Saberi knew many secrets. But his interrogators were interested in only one.
What did he know about Ron Arad?
Mr. Arad, an Israeli airman, vanished decades ago, and the Israeli military says he is the only service member classified as missing in action. The government’s long search for him has captivated the public and has come to symbolize Israel’s commitment, rooted in Jewish tradition, to bringing its soldiers home, dead or alive. Articles, books and documentaries have been produced about the hunt for Mr. Arad.
The Israeli government was so determined to find him that, even four decades after his disappearance, it took the risk of kidnapping General Saberi in the shadow of his own embassy.

nytimes.com.title: In Banff, a Grizzly Bear Known as ‘the Boss’ Rules the National Park
nytimes.com.text:
To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park he is grizzly bear 122. But to everyone who lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, and many of its 4.5 million annual visitors, he is the Boss.
He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect. He has shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and snacked on a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his 2,000-square-kilometer territory.
Most of all, the Boss has become Canada’s 700-pound celebrity bear king. When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, “bear jams” swiftly follow. His battles with a rival bear known as Split Lip are legendary. (He caused the split lip.) His annual awakening from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.
Galleries in Banff and neighboring Canmore ship giant photos of him worldwide. His image appears on fridge magnets, T-shirts and tote bags. A local restaurant is named for him, its main dining room dominated by a scrap metal sculpture of the bear.
But despite his fearsome demeanor, enhanced by four-inch claws, few bear experts consider the Boss a threat to park visitors or residents. Rather, they fear his celebrity and the legions of fans it have created, may be the biggest threat to his life and his dominance.

nytimes.com.title: Iran Attacks Bahrain for the Second Time in Days
nytimes.com.text:
Iran launched a drone attack against Bahrain on Sunday for the second time in days, as peace talks with the United States have faltered.
The Bahraini Defense Ministry said the Gulf Arab country’s armed forces had intercepted several “Iranian aerial threats” on Sunday before they struck their targets. Bahrain’s Interior Ministry also issued two alerts to residents on Sunday morning advising them to seek shelter.
There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed that Iranian forces had targeted a radar system at a Bahraini air base.
Bahrain separately hosts a major U.S. naval base. The American military did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Sunday’s attack came two days after the U.S. military said it had shot down two drones fired by Iran toward Bahrain, without causing any injuries or damage.
The Revolutionary Guards said that Friday’s attack was retaliation for a previous American strike on a telecommunications tower in Iran.
The attacks were the first to target Bahrain in about two months. After the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February, Iran launched thousands of retaliatory missile and drone attacks at Gulf Arab countries that host American military installations. But those attacks had largely petered out as the two sides entered a stalemate.

cnn.com.title: How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority
cnn.com.text: It’s a time-tested tradition: Presidents looking to reassert authority and escape political gloom head overseas for a global pick-me-up. Ever since 1982, when Ronald Reagan traded a recession, 11% unemployment and Democrats’ 26-seat pickup for a five-day swing through Latin America, Air Force One has been leaving political upheaval behind in its contrail. President Donald Trump will attempt to follow suit this week with a long-planned trip through Asia, punctuated Thursday by an unprecedented three-way meeting with his authoritarian counterparts from China and Russia — a splashy show of geopolitical theater alongside men whose power in their own countries goes mostly unchallenged. Comparisons with a newly constrained US leader may be unavoidable. The sharp rebuke Trump faced from voters this month was quickly clocked by his foreign counterparts, all watching closely for signs of fading political capital and early-onset lame-duck status. He’ll be joined on the trip by Elon Musk, whose $445 million in political spending failed to deliver Republican majorities. “Foreign policy and presidential trips are something only the president can do. There is pomp and circumstance. There’s a focus on it,” said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia who is now senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. “This is a way in which you start changing the narrative, and remind people that, you know, the president is still the president.” It’s not the only complication on Trump’s plate. The scandal involving Jensen Huang’s high-powered AI chips and affair with an alleged Chinese spy will loom over the US president’s visit to Shenzhen, the gleaming hub of China’s tech industry, even though Trump’s aides insist it wouldn’t dominate the journey. Trump doesn’t intend to raise the spying matter with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with whom he will meet for the fourth time in just over a year, American officials have previously told CNN. Officials said they also did not expect the two men to discuss the newly revived debate inside the administration over how to further restrict high-powered chips from going to China. “It’s probably not something we’re going to read the Chinese in on at the moment,” one senior US official said. Never particularly enthusiastic about grueling trips through far-flung time zones, Trump departs for the Philippines Monday after shaking up his West Wing leadership and facing calls even from some allies to fire members of his Cabinet, including the secretaries of Commerce and Defense. An air travel meltdown before he left — which Trump did not address publicly for days — also raised new questions about his mindset and focus heading into the trip. At two leaders summits — the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen — Trump will look to counter the narrative of his declining power by announcing new commercial deals and asserting American presence in a region that for decades has suffered from Washington’s inattention. Like his most recent predecessors, Trump has found the “pivot to Asia” an elusive concept. His second term became bogged down by a war in the Middle East, the same region that kept George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden from fully turning American foreign policy toward the Pacific. Trump has spent the past year working to cultivate deeper ties Xi. And he’s been seeking new trade deals, with plans to sign an agreement with Thailand this week, White House officials said. Yet the Iran war, along with Trump’s so-far futile efforts to end the war in Ukraine, continue to dominate his foreign policy agenda. Both are likely to hang over his talks this week in Asia, where fuel prices have spiked due to the conflicts. So, too, will Democrats’ stateside victories lead to questions of just how much Trump has left to offer. His two signature foreign policy initiatives — global tariffs and the Iran war — led to price increases that propelled voter anger toward him and Republicans. Democrats have vowed to limit his authorities on both, challenging the long-held adage that a president has a freer hand on foreign matters. A foreign trip has long been a way to drive home that point while also escaping Washington as the opposition prepares to assume power. Michael Deaver, an image-maker to Reagan, is credited with inventing the tactic when he arranged the Latin America trip in 1982. Nearly every president since then has replicated the idea. Bill Clinton made a trip to the Philippines in November 1994 after Republicans swept control of Congress for the first time in decades. George W. Bush was in Vietnam a few weeks after the GOP lost Congress in 2006. Barack Obama headed to Asia in 2010 and 2014 after midterm routs. And Trump himself made a somewhat desultory visit to France in 2017 after the GOP lost its majority in the House. “I’ve been with presidents immediately after midterm, both wins and losses, and it’s always important,” Kagan said. “It’s something that reminds the nation, it reminds foreign observers, that this is very much the president’s bailiwick.” For Trump, that means appearing in a joint setting with powerful men to discuss the world’s affairs. For some, the meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin carries unpleasant echoes of the 1945 conference in the Crimean resort of Yalta, where Stalin, Churchill and an extremely ill Franklin D. Roosevelt carved up the postwar world into western and eastern spheres of influence. Putin originally proposed the three-party summit as a venue to discuss the Ukraine war, where fraught issues of borders and sovereignty loom over nascent peace talks. Trump’s aides insist Thursday’s meeting is nothing of the sort, and say Ukraine won’t even be on the agenda. Instead, Trump hopes to open discussions on nuclear weapons with two leaders he’s worked hard to cultivate. The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia — which each have an estimated 5,000 warheads — expired in February. China, meanwhile, has been rapidly building its arsenal to more than 600 warheads but shows little interest in joining a pact. A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said expectations were low for a major breakthrough, describing the talks instead as a starting point. “It’s time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the official said. Xi had initially appeared skeptical of hosting the meeting, officials said, concerned it could overshadow the APEC summit and his attempts to showcase a rising China. But Trump, who sometimes says he envies authoritarians who rule as they wish, signed on quickly.

cnn.com.title: Showdown looms between Trump and Democrats over air traffic control meltdown
cnn.com.text: The shutdown that snarled American aviation last week showed that fixing the country’s antiquated air traffic control system could hardly be more urgent. But the political conditions needed to drag it into the 21st century look increasingly elusive. After thousands of delays and cancellations that disrupted the plans of more than a million people journeying to weddings, family events, funerals, work commitments and sports events, travel was nearing normality early Monday. But recriminations over the nationwide ground stop are escalating, with the Trump administration shifting blame and demanding tens of billions more in funding while newly empowered congressional Democrats warn there will be no blank check. Key questions include what caused the shutdown and whether it could happen again, especially with the traditional mass exodus at Thanksgiving looming; whether the White House has a plan and the capacity to fix the issue; how much will it cost to address; and how long it will take before a new system comes up to speed. Any successful modernization effort would require a unified national effort, bipartisan purpose, a president with political capital to catalyze action, and a government trusted to undertake big infrastructure projects. All this raises the question of whether the administrative machinery that won World War II and the Cold War is still capable of nimbly doing big things swiftly and on budget. The fallout from Friday’s ground stop suggests that few of those conditions exist, and the sudden exigency of upgrading the air traffic system will only heighten pressure on a lame-duck Congress that may struggle to keep the government open next month. Air traffic control funding and reform are also likely to become an early test of the hazardous political era that will dawn when Democrats run Congress next year opposite a GOP president. Trump finally weighs in Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy toured Sunday talk shows demanding action from Congress while assuring Americans they were safe in the air. “There hasn’t been investment in this network for decades … it’s the worst-kept secret in Washington. And the question becomes, well, when do we make the investments?” Duffy said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” A complicating factor is that the latest incident appears to have been caused by the act of modernizing the system itself. This only underscores the complexity of overhauling hardware that is already over-stressed by air traffic volumes it was not designed to accommodate while it remains in operation. Duffy told CNN the meltdown was triggered by an operation to change obsolete copper wire that apparently resulted in floods of data overwhelming the wider network. His explanation at least was an improvement on his imprecise White House news conference with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday, which produced few answers at a time when airports were mobbed by grounded travelers and then turned into a Trump-boosting session. “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin said, unironically, as chaos deepened and the commander in chief was most notable for his rare silence. Trump finally weighed in Sunday on Truth Social, blaming failures on the Biden administration and demanding Congress fund modernization with a huge package rather than in “drips and drabs.” But he seemed just as concerned with other priorities, including a judge’s order temporarily halting his plan to replace a beloved public golf links and park in Washington with a championship course. Friday’s graphic illustration of the air traffic control quandary might be the spur needed to prod Congress to act. But the president’s approach and record mean a new funding request will be contentious, especially when Democrats take over. The administration’s knee-jerk style of governing was on display Friday, when Duffy upped his request for funding from $30 billion to $50 billion without providing any details on why or how funds would be spent. Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer for the party’s leadership in the chamber, said it was “rich” for Duffy to complain since Congress had already given the administration what it wanted with $12 billion in Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill,” of which only a third had been spent. “I will support whatever level of money is necessary to fix this problem. We should fix this problem on a bipartisan basis,” Van Hollen said on “State of the Union.” But he warned, “If they need more, they should come up and justify it.” Democratic Rep. Jim Himes claimed the administration had helped cause the debacle, blaming Elon Musk for forcing 1,300 Federal Aviation Administration employees to retire or resign and firing 400 probationary employees as part of Department of Government Efficiency purges last year. “What you’re seeing is the wages of what Elon Musk did, where he just gutted an entity that affected millions of Americans last Friday,” Himes said on CBS’ “Face the Nation.” Does Trump have the bandwidth to fix the problem? The Trump administration’s recent struggles and controversies hardly enhance confidence in its capacity to govern effectively and to fix air traffic control. The far easier task of restoring the Reflecting Pool on Washington’s National Mall — a Trump pet project — turned into a farce. The White House is currently gripped by a scandal over Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief instrumental to shaping Trump’s AI policy who resigned over extramarital affairs, including with a woman described by a US official as a potential Chinese intelligence asset. Meanwhile, Trump still hasn’t ended a war with Iran he promised would take mere weeks. It flared up again this weekend and will shortly head into its 10th month. And on Friday, the Pan American Health Organization determined that the US no longer qualified as having eliminated measles. The loss of public trust in Trump was underscored by the GOP’s disastrous losses in the midterm elections. The administration’s failure in some cases to spend money appropriated by Congress on its intended purpose will bolster demands from lawmakers for strict conditions attached to any new funding. Duffy is quite correct to say that underfunding and delays in upgrading air traffic control have been a common thread across multiple administrations. But there is growing concern over the current White House’s management of the situation. A report by the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan federal agency, warned in September that while the FAA had made progress in modernizing outdated air traffic control systems, “it could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions.” The report warned that the FAA lacked a lifecycle cost estimate or master schedule for related projects — a failing it said could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems. No one could argue that Friday’s emergency came as a surprise. Lawmakers and administrations have been warning for decades that the system is old and overburdened, and its problems speak to a wider failure to overhaul critical infrastructure. Trump has often compared US airports unfavorably with modern travel facilities in China and in the developing world. But modernization efforts in the US are often hampered by infighting in Congress and a dysfunctional budget process as the government careens between shutdown crises and fiscal cliffs. While Trump put the blame on Biden, Republican majorities have regularly clipped funding requests for aviation industry modernization from Democratic presidents. In 2011, Van Hollen, then a member of the House, warned that “our nation’s aviation infrastructure critically needs rehabilitation” and accused GOP leaders of paring back funding to 2008 levels. In 2015, President Barack Obama’s Budget Director Shaun Donovan warned Republicans that their $255 million cut to a $2.6 billion FAA request would slow modernization that “would lead to worsening air traffic delays and higher replacement costs in the future.” In 2025, Democrats raised concerns about Trump’s $12.5 billion FAA request, warning that even Capitol Hill Republicans and those in the White House were divided on priorities. “Before we pour billions into the nation’s air traffic control system, we should ensure we have the policies, implementation plan, timing, and funding level right so we are not throwing hard-earned taxpayer money at projects and programs that will not actually fix the problem,” Democratic committee members wrote in a letter to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation panel’s chairman Ted Cruz. Last week’s debacle at America’s airports will heighten such questions and may degenerate into a confrontation between a Democratic Congress and a Republican president next year. Illinois Democratic Sen. Tammy Duckworth accused Republicans of finding money for Trump’s vanity projects during two years in control of Congress. “But none to fix our air traffic control system? Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch,” she wrote on X. But Duffy is pleading for help “I have systems that are from the ’90s. I have radar that are from the ‘60s and ‘70s,” he told CNN. “We can fight about all kinds of things in America, but let’s not fight about this.” In theory, an air traffic control emergency that could compromise the safety of every American flyer is crying out for bipartisan compromise. The question now therefore is whether the nation’s deep and enduring polarization will again thwart efforts to solve one of its most pressing crises.

cnn.com.title: Army soldier files whistleblower complaint against the Pentagon over Iranian strike that killed 6 US service members
cnn.com.text: One of the US Army soldiers that survived an Iranian strike that hit a makeshift operations center in Kuwait and killed six has submitted a whistleblower complaint alleging that the Pentagon did not listen to concerns about the lack of proper protection for troops, according to a copy of the disclosure obtained by CNN. The complaint, submitted last week to the House and Senate Armed Services committees and first reported by CBS, comes as Democrats are poised to launch wide-ranging investigations into the Trump administration and its handling of the Iran war when they take control of Congress in January. CNN has reached out to the congressional committees and the Pentagon for comment. Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom outlined why he submitted the report in an exclusive interview with CBS’ Norah O’Donnell on “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday, describing the March 1 attack as a “tactical failure” by “the Army, our leadership, and myself.” “We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn,” he said. He added that some people described the operations center as a “trailer park.” The six US Army Reserve soldiers killed in the strike at Kuwait’s Shuaiba port were the first US service members killed in the US’ war with Iran. Dozens, including Ramsbottom, were wounded. While senior Pentagon officials said at the time that the building was fortified, a source familiar with the site previously told CNN it was only surrounded by concrete barriers that would provide protection from car bombs but had nothing to shield it from drones or missiles. CNN also previously reported that the attack came quickly and with no warning or sirens to alert troops to evacuate or get into a bunker, according to a source familiar with the situation. Ramsbottom said he brought up the lack of protection from aerial attacks to his superiors in various meetings and was told: “We don’t have to worry about protection.” Military leaders later said that they were going to try to get a counter-drone system sent to the site, but “it never arrived at Shuaiba and we don’t know if it was ever even ordered to or requested,” he said. The installation did not have a physician or a fixed aid station when the drone strike happened, according to the whistleblower report. There was only one ambulance at the site. Ramsbottom has made similar claims in interviews with multiple outlets since the attack. In an interview with CNN affiliate KOAA news in April, he recalled that while the facility had protections for “legacy threats” like mortar fire or car bombs, it wasn’t prepared for modern drone warfare. “It was well-fortified for that type of thinking from pre-Russian invasion of Ukraine. It was a pretty well fortified base. But it wasn’t well prepared for the type of fight that we’re getting into,” he told the news station. At a press conference after the attack in March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the US has “incredible air defenders,” but acknowledged that “one” projectile had made it through in the attack. “Every once in a while you might have one — unfortunately, we call it a squirter — that makes its way through. And in that particular case, it happened to hit a tactical operation center that was, that was fortified, but it — these are powerful weapons,” he said. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who sits on the House Armed Services Committee and is the top Democrat on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has asked Hegseth to appear in a classified briefing to answer questions and provide “all force protection assessments” about the facility at the Shuaiba port.

cnn.com.title: Notorious Mexican drug lord, who was convicted of killing US DEA agent, dies at 80
cnn.com.text: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels whose conviction for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers, died in hospital on Sunday at age 80. Local security authorities said Félix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died around 2 p.m. on Sunday. Imprisoned since 1989, Félix Gallardo was an inmate in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health. Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in ensuing decades. His rise and fall was portrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 hit Netflix series “Narcos: Mexico.” Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and bodyguard for a local governor then became a powerful criminal capo known as the “boss of bosses.” Félix Gallardo and others set up the cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and to forge an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar’s Medellin cartel. His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials and innovations like using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero. His legal battles stretched across decades. Arrested in 1989, Félix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel. While already incarcerated, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar. Camarena’s killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressed Mexico hard to arrest those involved. In 2017, a federal court found Félix Gallardo guilty in that case and imposed a further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings. Félix Gallardo suffered poor health in his final years, and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence. “Thirty-two years have passed… That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime,” he said.

cnn.com.title: Trump, McDonald’s and Burger King among targets of past X posts that contain redirected website links
cnn.com.text: Some website links included in the X posts of politicians, government agencies and companies were redirected this weekend to unrelated videos, images and websites. Links dating as far back as 2009 from URL-shortening service Bitly were affected, and only corporate and political X accounts appear to have been targeted, with President Donald Trump’s personal account seemingly hit the hardest. At least a dozen of Trump’s posts on X now direct to various inappropriate and unrelated sites. Public figures — like Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and former Vice President Mike Pence — as well as fast-food chains McDonald’s and Burger King, were also hit to varying degrees. Bitly URLs are shortened while holding the original and longer link. Bitly links do not automatically expire, according to the company’s website, but paid users can redirect links. Bitly said Sunday afternoon in a post on X that it had “identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts.” The company said it suspended the accounts that altered links and were working to disable the affected URLs. “Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the issue and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future,” Bitly wrote. Both Bitly and X have not yet responded to CNN’s request for comment. It’s unclear whether hackers made custom Bitly links, which effectively allow them to copy the original URL and redirect to any website. That may have been possible if the original Bitly link to the website no longer exists or has expired. Bitly links may be susceptible to artificial intelligence scans and exploiting mechanisms to redirect links, noted Ari Lightman, a digital media professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy. The redirected links seem confined to posts made between 2009 and 2014. Lightman said that some social media accounts are not monitored, “and that’s problematic.” Changing unmonitored links could expose user information when clicking those links, he warned, highlighting the importance of internet safety. “You have a variety of vulnerabilities that people can utilize for exploitation,” said Lightman. “It’s just finding these old messages out there and sort of repopulating them,” often for malicious purposes. A 2013 post from Trump criticizing wind turbines that used a Bitly link now redirects to a Google site titled “fortnite baby” and includes a photo of a baby. Another 2013 post from Trump tagged former Republican nominee for president Mitt Romney, and links to the popular game “Geometry Dash.” One of Trump’s posts about his golf course in Scotland includes a link to an Epstein files Wikipedia page. “It sounds like they’re trying to make some sort of a message tying these sites into Donald Trump’s policies, and sometimes it’s just vulgar mechanisms,” said Lightman. Public officials and company heads who often circulated Bitly links were also targeted. A post in 2010 from Microsoft founder Bill Gates contains the text, “Notes from D.C. trip. Spoke w/former President Clinton at the Foreign Relations committee aid programs are working,” and includes a Bitly link of a Reddit page that has an animated image from a fabricated posting by former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg. A post in 2011 by Trudeau contains a Bitly link that redirects to a vulgar YouTube audio clip. A 2011 post from Burger King intended to provide restaurant locations was redirected to a Wikipedia page on a list of Nazi concentration camps, while another post linked to a Wikipedia page on Adolf Hitler. McDonald’s account has a post from 2011 that redirected to a page about the September 11 attacks, while its Indonesia account made a 2013 post about a jingle that now links to an unrelated “Would you rather?” YouTube video. A spokesperson for Burger King told CNN the company has “no part in the links being redirected” and that it was “working quickly to correct and delete posts that have been altered.” McDonald’s did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment. Government accounts have also been ironically affected. A 2012 post from the FBI about computers infected by “Ghost Clicks” now directs to a page with a photo of a seal, while the Department of Defense account had a separately redirected post. A post by Pence seemingly directed to the same website as the FBI, despite being about an unrelated topic. Hijacking these links is especially concerning in the age of AI, says Lightman, because it allows manipulations to be made “en masse.”

cnn.com.title: In newly blue Texas, far-right Christian nationalists gather to plan a future after Trump
cnn.com.text: Disillusioned by President Donald Trump, hundreds of people gathered in newly blue Texas this weekend for a far-right Christian nationalist conference to discuss a path forward to advance their agenda after major Republican defeats in the midterm elections. Many of the attendees at the conference, entitled “Christ is King: America After Trump,” had voted for Trump in the last three elections but now no longer support him and are at odds with much of the Republican Party. While some conservative Christians back America’s war with Iran and US support of Israel, among the far-right faction that gathered here in Irving this weekend, Trump’s decision to go to war was the ultimate act of betrayal. Speakers at the event promoted antisemitic tropes, discussed the need for the United States to remain a majority White nation, argued Christianity should have precedence over other religions in this country, called for mass deportations, and pondered revoking the 19th Amendment, which guaranteed women the right to vote. Much of this was welcomed with rapturous applause and standing ovations from the overwhelmingly male audience. The far-right streamer Nick Fuentes, an online firebrand known for his unapologetic racist, antisemitic, and sexist takes, delivered an hourlong speech at the event’s close on Saturday. Other speakers included the conspiracy theorist Alex Jones and Buckley Carlson, the brother of Tucker Carlson. Fuentes rarely appears in public, instead electing to stream his show nightly from home and appear on other people’s podcasts, but on Saturday he spoke of the need for he and his followers, known as “groypers,” to mobilize ahead of the 2028 election. “The midterms were a rejection of Donald Trump. They were not a rejection of Trump-ism. And this is maybe the most important point,” Fuentes said. “100,000 groypers doesn’t flip the country 50% in favor of our ideology, but 100,000 groypers can do 100 million phone calls. They can knock on 100 million doors. We can get out there in the Iowa caucus,” Fuentes added. It is difficult to determine how big Fuentes’ following is, but his nightly stream regularly is viewed hundreds of thousands of times, and young men who openly identify as groypers are now often seen at conservative events wearing Fuentes merchandise. Some Fuentes fans CNN spoke to at the event on Saturday had traveled across the country to see the 28-year-old streamer speak. In 2022, Fuentes joined Trump and Kanye West (now known as “Ye”) for dinner at Mar-a-Lago. Trump later said he had no idea who Fuentes was. This weekend’s event took place at the Irving Convention Center near Dallas and was sponsored by NXR Studios, a far-right Christian nationalist media company, Joel Webbon, a preacher who runs NXR, delivered a speech rife with antisemitism, racism, and misogyny where he outlined his vision for a United States where White Christian men reign supreme. “We’re done with equality,” Webbon said, despite the First Amendment to the US Constitution’s prohibition on the government favoring one religion over another. “Christianity is American. Islam is not, Hinduism is not, Judaism is not,” he proclaimed to applause. Ten years ago, MAGA was the insurgent movement that pulled the Republican Party further to the right. The cohort who gathered in Texas this weekend believe MAGA didn’t go far-right enough, and Fuentes pointed to the recent success of democratic socialists on the left as a model for a successful insurgent movement within the post-Trump Republican Party. “My model actually is the DSA,” Fuentes said, “It’s the Zohran Mamdanis, Abdul El-Sayeds.” But Fuentes and company may have difficulty building a successful political coalition given the sheer number of people they hope to one day exclude from the political process. “Every time you see a woman in leadership, I guarantee, there were at least a thousand men who were more qualified for that position than her,” Webbon said on stage, before reminding the audience he is in favor of revoking women’s right to vote.

cnn.com.title: As Trump administration implores Congress for additional FAA funding, Democrats say the agency already has it
cnn.com.text: Following a historic airspace meltdown on Friday that grounded all flights nationwide, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has implored Congress to authorize tens of billions of dollars in additional funding for the Federal Aviation Administration. But Democrats, who are set to take the majority in January, are pointing to  legislation passed by Republicans last year that already gave the agency $12.5 billion, arguing that it already has the funds it needs. Duffy says that’s not true. “I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom. I can’t build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s, but there’s no money for that. There’s no money for towers. Our towers are old,” Duffy said on CNN’s “State of the Union” with Dana Bash on Sunday. Duffy had asked Congress for around $30 billion but after Friday’s incident, he upped the request to $50 billion. President Donald Trump, in a social media post on Sunday, also urged Congress to “give the money, FAST!” The transportation secretary said the ground stop was likely due to an issue that occurred while contractor L3Harris was switching an old copper wire at an air traffic location in El Dorado, Arkansas, to a more modern fiber optic system. It is unclear whether the outage was due to faulty equipment or contractor error. Of the $12.5 billion given to the agency for three years under Trump’s massive spending and policy bill — which no Democrats supported — $4.75 billion was allocated for “telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades.” Duffy said at a news conference Saturday that the agency has spent about one-third of the modernization budget so far. On Sunday, Duffy said all the telecom work can be done by “the first part of 2029.” “All I need is the money to finish it. And my, my hope is that if they give me money today, I’ll be going tomorrow to build it,” Duffy said. Later Saturday, Reps. Rick Larsen and André Carson — the top Democrats on two House panels overseeing the aviation industry — asked the administration to explain to Congress why the agency needs more money if there are still unspent funds. The two added in a joint statement that FAA and DOT employees will brief their staff on Monday. Meanwhile, some Democrats slammed the administration’s priorities and how it has spent money in immigration enforcement and construction projects in Washington, DC, over aviation modernization and safety. “There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA,” Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz said in a post on X. “We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars.” Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth said in a post on X, “You’ve literally controlled Congress for the past two years. And apparently, there’s always been money for vanity projects. But none to fix our air traffic control system? Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch.” Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the House Appropriations Committee’s top Democrat, called Duffy’s $50 billion request a “ransom.” “Our air traffic controllers have been failed by Secretary Duffy,” DeLauro said in a post on X, adding, “We need a competent partner at DOT.” However, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who launched a bid for Senate majority leader last week, signaled openness to supporting additional funds for the agency on Sunday while calling on administration officials to come to Congress and “justify” the ask. “I will support whatever level of money is necessary to fix this problem. We should fix this problem on a bipartisan basis,” Hollen told CNN on Sunday, but added, “It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for. If they need more, they should come up and justify it.” Republicans could use the remaining weeks of their majority to approve additional funding for the agency, and outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson said Saturday that he would add FAA funding to an upcoming “legislative package.” “We don’t really need any investigation to understand we need further investment,” Johnson told Fox News. “We’re going to work to get it done.” It was not immediately clear to congressional aides how leaders will pass new funding. Currently, appropriators are negotiating a government funding deal ahead of a December 11 deadline. Senate leadership aides in each party did not immediately respond to questions about the path forward in that chamber. GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt is also pushing for passage of his bill, the Modern Skies Act, which would invest $30 billion in modernizing the nation’s aviation system. The Missouri senator spoke with Trump on Friday, and has also spoken with Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on the topic.

cnn.com.title: Behind the scenes of Scott Colom’s viral ‘pick another protein’ ad
cnn.com.text: Russ Hudson of Columbus, Mississippi, became one of the unexpected stars of the 2026 midterms, with a feature role in an ad that’s since been viewed more than 20 million times on X alone – tipping his head back and exclaiming, “sheeeit.” “It’s been crazy. Like, I never expected it to do this,” Hudson told CNN in an interview, reflecting on the ad for Democratic Sen.-elect Scott Colom that helped spark one of the biggest political upsets of the election cycle. Posted to social media on October 13, the ad features Hudson and other Mississippians rebuking incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith for suggesting there are many other proteins to chose from when pressed on high beef prices. “Pick another protein, sheeeit,” Hudson says in the spot as he grills burgers. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.” “When I originally told Scott I would do it, I thought maybe like 100, maybe 1,000 views at most,” Hudson said. “I never expected it to do what it did. And I didn’t have TikTok. I literally had to download TikTok to see what all the hype was about because a bunch of my friends were sending messages like, ‘Dude, you’re like worldwide.’” Hudson said that he’d been recognized in public a few times and asked for pictures, “like I’m some superstar or something.” “So it’s a little weird. I’m not used to that, obviously,” he said. Hudson, the father of a four-month-old infant and an Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, said that he’d known Colom for a decade, and that his sister had worked with him. The initial plan called for Hudson’s father to appear in the ad, but he was reluctant to curse on camera, so the younger Russ volunteered. “I just went to his mom’s house in the backyard, and we fired up the grill, and they gave me the lines, and we just rolled with it,” Hudson said. For the signature line – the “s-h-e-e-e-i-t,” as Hudson spells it – he said they did about ten to fifteen takes, but that Colom said he nailed it on the third. “That’s something we say. And my buddy was talking to me on the phone the other day, and he said something. I was like, ‘sheeeit!’ He was like, ‘There you go.’ It’s just a thing, man,” Hudson laughed. Underscoring the ad’s point, Hudson also recalled saving the burgers he’s seen flipping on the grill. “[Colom] told me to save the burgers because beef prices were high. So, I didn’t want to waste them,” Hudson said. Asked what he thought of the comment from Hyde-Smith that started it all, telling Mississippians to pick another protein, Hudson said that “it’s ridiculous.” “We deserve better than that, and that’s why one of the reasons I really wanted to back Scott, you know, because I mean he wants to make things affordable for us here in Mississippi,” Hudson said. He also considered the landmark victory, saying that “it’s pretty cool – I know it’s gonna go down in history. My mom keeps reminding me of that, and I’m just like, yeah, it’s pretty cool to be a part of that.” “But the main thing is, is the goal was to help Scott win this election, and it did that,” he said, crediting the advertisement’s writers and producers for “all the work.” As for what he’ll remember from the experience, Hudson paused for a moment. “The Mississippi folks will appreciate this,” Hudson said, before referencing musician Doughbelly Stray. “[He] did a song one time that says, ‘My Mississippi ain’t on this map,’ and our Mississippi’s on this map now. So that’s what I remember from it as we put Mississippi on the map,” he said. Ryan Sayles, the creative mind behind the ad, joined CNN’s “The Arena with Kasie Hunt” on Thursday and shared more details on the production. Saying he wanted to bring a “Mississippi feel to it,” Sayles instructed the individuals reading the lines to “drag it out so people can really feel how you feel.” He also picked the catchy backing track – “Rapper’s Delight” by Sugarhill Gang – crediting his dad’s influence as a former DJ. “I was a class clown, you know. I joke a lot, so I definitely think that this helped people look at it and say, “Oh man, this is funny,” but that’s really how I feel, you know,” Sayles said, underlining the importance of humor in political messaging. “Like it was funny, but it wasn’t funny, you know what I mean? It was a good way to just get attention and bring national attention to Mississippi.” And Sayles praised Colom for his engagement with the process and willingness to take risks, saying that “he thinks about how he can reach people that normally wouldn’t be reached.” Eight days after Election Day, CNN projected that Colom would defeat Hyde-Smith, becoming the first Democrat elected to the US Senate in Mississippi in more than four decades. The outcome ranks as perhaps the most stunning upset in an election cycle full of historic wins as Democrats capitalized on sharp voter backlash to the Trump administration. In a nod to the viral ad at his victory party last week, Colom stood at a lectern behind a sign that read “picked another senator” as he thanked Mississippians for their support.

cnn.com.title: Russian diesel under Trump deal struggles to reach US market amid legal fears and criticism
cnn.com.text: More than a month after President Donald Trump announced a surprise deal to import Russian diesel, the oil has struggled to reach the US market amid outrage and legal concerns. Several oil tankers that departed from a key Russian oil-loading port — and are believed to be laden with diesel — are no longer bound for the US, according to ship tracking data from MarineTraffic, and US businesses and ports have steered clear of accepting Russian diesel for fear of legal and reputational risks, experts told CNN. Bipartisan lawmakers and European allies expressed outrage at the agreement that Trump said he reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin to bring tens of thousands of barrels of Russian diesel into US and global markets. They condemned it as a concession to Russia as it continued its war against Ukraine and warned that those who imported the diesel could run afoul of international sanctions and US law. One of the tankers, Agioi Fanendes, departed Russia with tens of thousands of barrels of Russian diesel. Its destination was listed as the Port of New York and New Jersey, and it was initially expected to arrive around November 7. As of Sunday, the vessel was hovering hundreds of miles off the eastern coast of the US. It was officially broadcasting “FOR ORDERS” instead of a destination port. A spokesperson for Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited, the company that operates the tanker, told CNN on Thursday that its “discharging port is not confirmed yet.” Several other oil tankers that departed Primorsk — one of Russia’s largest oil-loading ports — in mid-October have also shifted away from the US, according to data from MarineTraffic reviewed by CNN. One, the Talisman, docked at the Port of Alexandria in Egypt in recent days. Another, the Leruo, is now heading to Brazil. They had earlier declared their destinations as the US Atlantic coast. Both vessels are under European and British sanctions, and the Talisman is also sanctioned in the US. A White House official told CNN on Wednesday that “consistent with the deal agreed to between President Trump and President Putin, Russian diesel is on the water and heading to the market, which will ease prices for Americans.” The official did not say the diesel was heading to the US. The person said the deal “was made to add diesel supply to the global market — lowering prices for Americans and the world — which is exactly what will be done.” Trump announced in a social media post on October 9 that he had reached a deal with Putin for Russia to “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” The administration billed the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections amid steep fuel costs, as a way to lower prices for US consumers. Experts said the diesel would have little to no impact on prices, and amounts to less than a day of US energy consumption. Questions about legality of importing Russian fuel Last month, a group of bipartisan lawmakers sent letters to the CEOs of JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, and the heads of Port Authorities of New York/New Jersey and of Houston, Corpus Christi and Beaumont, Texas, warning that they could face legal action if they are involved in importing the Russian diesel into the US. The Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022 bans Russian-origin energy products, including diesel fuel, from being imported into the US “unless — following a period for consultation with Congress — the President certifies to Congress that Russia has ceased military hostilities in Ukraine, that Russia poses no immediate military threat to NATO members, and that Russia recognizes the right of Ukrainians to choose their government,” the lawmakers warned. Although the US Treasury Department issued a sanctions waiver to allow the import of the diesel under the deal between the Trump administration and Moscow, the lawmakers consider that sanctions waiver to defy the law. “Any importation of Russian diesel into the U.S. raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations,” wrote Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Coons, Elizabeth Warren, GOP Sen. Thom Tillis, and Democratic Rep. Gregory Meeks. “Criminal penalties may apply to any company that knowingly buys Russian diesel or facilitates its importation, and not simply the importer of record,” they wrote. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill warned her state’s port and terminal operators last week that “any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.” Charles Lichfield, the director of economic foresight and analysis and the C. Boyden Gray senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center, noted that US importers would face “the immediate reputational risk” as well as the legal ramifications. He noted that a general license from the Treasury Department, which allows businesses to import the diesel without fear of sanctions, would appear to be good protection but the 2022 law is still on the books, which raises questions about legality and the potential for prosecution down the line. “All of this is very politically charged (and) the volumes are small,” he said. “You could make a few million dollars off this shipment, but is it really worth it?” Julian Hayda, the associate director for advocacy at the organization Razom for Ukraine, noted that “now that Democrats have control of both chambers of Congress, they are most certainly going to launch investigations into these companies, so it’s not going to be worth it for many of these companies to buy this vehicle in and when it arrives on American shores.” This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Meet the miso-making engineer behind Anthropic’s biggest hit
cnn.com.text: Boris Cherny loves to code. So much, in fact, that he once said coding is the reason most people choose to become engineers in the first place. He’s also the reason why many tech workers may never have to write a line of code again. Cherny, 35, is the creator of Claude Code, the wildly popular Anthropic coding agent that’s made the company a driving AI force. The agent can write code, run commands, and access files to accomplish work on a user’s behalf. Claude Code was a hit with programmers and non-programmers alike in Silicon Valley, giving Anthropic an early foothold in the workplace. The tool also paved the way for Anthropic’s AI tools to play a larger role in industries like finance, legal work, marketing and more. Anthropic’s success has thrust the company into the middle of both the anxieties and optimism about AI’s impact on future jobs, and Cherny has embraced his place in that discussion. “I think for the job market, in particular for engineers, it will be disruptive,” Cherny said in an interview with CNN earlier this year. “I hope that over the long term, it’s amazing for humanity and what it unlocks.” Anthropic’s expected more than trillion-dollar initial public offering hinges on whether it can succeed in making Claude indispensable to office work. And it all started with Cherny’s Claude Code. “When people think about the IPO, they’re thinking, ‘Okay, how much room left does Claude Code have to grow?’” Willy Lee, principal at venture capital firm Neostellar, whose portfolio includes OpenAI and CoreWeave, told CNN. Here’s how Cherny, whose official title is head of applications, became a critical part of Anthropic and the broader discourse over AI’s impact on jobs. The rise of Claude Code Cherny joined Anthropic in 2024 after a nearly seven-year run at Meta, where he worked in various divisions, including Instagram, Facebook Groups and the code quality team, according to his LinkedIn. In 2022, during his Meta tenure, he and his wife temporarily moved to Japan for her work. Across the world from his colleagues in California, Cherny loved being able to code all day without the interruptions of meetings and project management tasks, he said on an episode of the tech industry podcast “The Peterman Pod” in 2025. He was one of the few engineers in Meta’s Instagram division who was coding so much. “For me, when I write code, I have an emotional relationship with it, and it’s something I think about when I’m really deep in a problem,” he said on the podcast. “I dream about it.” He spent a month experimenting with Anthropic’s models after joining the company, he told “Lenny’s Podcast,” a show about product development. In his early days at Anthropic, he mostly built prototypes to test the boundaries of what the Claude maker’s AI could do. But he reached a turning point a couple of months later when he created a command-line interface tool for Claude, which enabled the AI helper to interact directly with his computer’s operating system. Cherny made a simple request: figure out what music he was listening to. He was shocked when the tool wrote code to answer that question without being specifically told to do so. “The model was given this tool, and it figured out how to use it to answer this question that I had that I wasn’t even sure it could answer,” he said on “Lenny’s Podcast.” That side project laid the foundation for Claude Code, which surpassed $2.5 billion in run-rate revenue in February. Anthropic doesn’t disclose usage numbers for Claude Code, but a chart in the company’s S-1 filing ahead of its IPO shows revenue ramping up following Claude Code’s release. For Cherny, expanding Claude Code’s reach involves talking to real people about how they use the product. On X, Cherny replies to questions from Claude users on a weekly — sometimes almost daily — basis. It’s a habit he formed long before joining Anthropic. When he worked at Meta in California, he often showed the cafeteria workers new features to see if they were able to figure them out quickly, he told “The Peterman Pod.” “The thing that actually excites me is talking to people and understanding how we can make the product better,” he told CNN in March. “I’m just completely focused on that.” Claude Code’s effect on the AI market Enterprise AI spending accelerated in late 2025 following Claude Code’s release to the general public in May, said Ara Kharazian, senior economist at financial services company Ramp, which tracks business spending on AI. “That was the first commercially advanced version of AI that was directly productivity enhancing for a specific segment of jobs,” he said of Claude Code and other coding agents. Anthropic’s coding tool served as a jumping-off point for Claude Cowork, the company’s AI agent for general office work that can manage files and automate tasks. The idea for Cowork came after Cherny observed people and companies using Claude Code for non-technical duties. Cherny himself uses it for paying parking tickets and project management work for his team at Anthropic, he said on “Lenny’s Podcast.” Non-technical employees at the Mid-Ohio Food Collective frequently use Claude Code, according to Mark Mollenkopf, the organization’s director of software engineering. Its director of nutrition used Claude Code to build a game that’s like Tinder for food, aiming to help families choose healthier options based on their preferences. They had the idea for nearly a decade; Mollenkopf says he still has photos of a whiteboard with the initial concept from 2017. But the team has been too busy with higher priority tasks until it’s been able to have Claude Code handle it. “We’re not going to put it in production today yet, but it’s that unlock for us to be able to democratize great ideas that we’ve always had,” Mollenkopf said. Anthropic built Claude Cowork in 10 days using Claude Code. It shows how important Cherny’s brainchild has been for Anthropic’s own growth, not just drawing in more customers. Still, the company faces myriad challenges, including increased competition from OpenAI, reliance on a limited number of customers and pressure to live up to its sky-high valuation. The future of work Meanwhile, Anthropic has played a fundamental yet complicated role in the AI boom. The company has warned about the risks of AI, saying it’s capable of catastrophic consequences, yet it continues to charge ahead with new models. It worries that the economy isn’t ready for AI’s impact on jobs, yet it creates and iterates on tools like Claude Code and Claude Cowork for automating work. Cherny is at the center of that paradox. Some software engineers have grown increasingly wary of AI’s role in their jobs, with six in 10 tech workers saying they actively try to avoid using AI, according to a recent survey of 30,000 programmers conducted by tech site Stack Overflow. Some believe the tech isn’t as capable as it’s been made out to be, while others feel AI’s role in tech has led to more burnout over the pressure to perform and stay up to date on the newest technologies. Cherny has a lot of thoughts about what the future looks like. The job of a software engineer already involves doing a lot more than just coding; it entails working with designers and other teams, and figuring out what to build next. As AI takes over most coding tasks, engineers will be freed up to focus on these other parts of the job, he said. That’s why he said in March that he thinks software engineering jobs are going to start disappearing by the end of this year. “The (job) title will be maybe ‘builder,’” he told CNN. “Maybe we’ll still call them software engineers, but they’re going to do much more than engineers do today.” Cherny has emerged as somewhat of an icon among developers and engineers like Mollenkopf, who said he watches podcasts featuring the Claude Code creator and others in similar roles to learn more about AI. That’s how Mollenkopf learned about Claude Tag, a feature that lets users connect work data to Claude and then tag the AI helper in Slack. Mollenkopf said he would be “a total fanboy” if he could ever meet Cherny. What Cherny can’t predict is how long that shift could take. It’s almost the end of 2026, and software engineering jobs still exist – although they likely look different than they did several years ago. But if there’s one thing he learned during his time in Japan, it’s how to think long-term. He remembers learning to make miso, a traditional Japanese seasoning made by fermenting grains like soybeans and barley, to bond with his neighbors. It’s a hobby that starkly contrasted the fast-paced tech world Cherny was used to: a single batch could take months to make. “Miso is this interesting thing where it teaches you to think on these long-time skills,” he said. “…You just have to be very patient.”

cnn.com.title: Estonia to shut its border with Russia, blaming Moscow for foiled arson plot
cnn.com.text: Estonia is to close its border with Russia after blaming Moscow for a suspected attack on a defense technology company, Estonia’s prime minister said Sunday. Eight people have been detained after allegedly attempting an arson attack on the company overnight on Saturday, authorities say. No one was injured. Estonian security services say the attempted attack was carried out on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU. “If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face,” Prime Minister Kristen Michal said in a statement Sunday. “Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defense industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable,” he added. Border crossings will be closed from December 1, and Michal did not say when they would reopen. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Russian state news agency TASS that the move is part of a wider pattern of “Russophobia.” “We’ll check all this for veracity,” Zakharova said. “But if these are their real plans, then they’re part of another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia.” Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the “attempted sabotage” this weekend was “yet another reminder that Russia’s hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine” and that “hostile actions must have consequences.” He said he expected further sanctions to be adopted targeting Russian individuals and entities at a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Brussels, Belgium on Monday. Ukraine has commended Estonia for its move to close the border, hailing it as an example of effective action against Russian hostility and encouraging Europe to take note. “Estonia has shown that Russian sabotage can and should have consequences beyond diplomatic condemnation,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X. “This approach deserves wider support across Europe.” Russia has long been accused of carrying out sabotage and other hybrid attacks against Europe but has repeatedly denied the claims. Back in September, European officials pointed the finger at the Kremlin following a series of incidents that appeared to target NATO members. A railway line on which several former Western diplomats were traveling was struck by a Russian drone near Ukraine’s border with Poland, while another drone – likely of Russian origin – was shot down in Lithuania. A third drone also washed ashore in Poland. Elsewhere, a Danish helicopter was narrowly missed by a Russian flare, and Dutch rail traffic was significantly disrupted after metal pipes that had been fitted across the tracks triggered short circuits, turned traffic signals to red and forced trains to an inconvenient stop. Despite denying involvement, Moscow has remained the alleged culprit. European NATO-member allies have deemed the actions an escalation of conflict against the bloc – characterizing the attacks as measures designed to antagonize without triggering all-out war.

cnn.com.title: Iran raises stakes with new drone attacks as Trump signals a waiting game
cnn.com.text: Gulf states have been worried for weeks that Iran may again begin to target them in an effort to force a resolution to the nine-month regional conflict on its terms. In the past few days, that anxiety has deepened with two attempted drone attacks on Bahrain, an American ally that hosts major US military facilities, while Tehran has also warned the Gulf states not to “reopen old wounds.” Iran appears to be raising the stakes as it struggles to prevent more Gulf oil and gas from getting through the Strait of Hormuz as its economy labors under US blockade and the cumulative effect of international sanctions. The Bahrain Defense Force said Sunday it had “intercepted and destroyed” several Iranian drones, after a similar interception on Friday. The US Embassy in Bahrain on Sunday urged Americans to exercise “heightened vigilance,” citing an increased threat of attacks by Iran-backed Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US government officials and facilities in the region. The embassy also warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions, while noting that it remained open. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had earlier claimed an attack on a US helicopter base in Bahrain, saying it was in retaliation for unspecified US “aggression.” CNN has reached out to US Central Command for comment.
