The targeting of Bahrain has accompanied a more belligerent tone out of Tehran toward Iran’s neighbors, the consequences of renewed US or Israeli strikes and the state of negotiations with the US. Iran was incensed by suggestions from the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) last week that it would have to pay its neighbors compensation for attacks on their territory, something Iran itself is seeking in any deal with the US. “How can countries that actively participated in military aggression against a neighboring country and made their airspace, territory and waters available to those who attacked Iranian territory speak of seeking compensation from Iran?” asked foreign mxfinistry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei in a news conference on Sunday. “What about Iran’s inherent and legal right to defend itself?” In a reminder that Iran does not forget the past, Baghaei said the Gulf states “must be careful not to reopen old wounds,” referring to their support for Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in the war with Iran in the 1980s. Iran wants the Gulf states “to pay the price for a war they did not choose, then give up their right to accountability and compensation. This is an equation that cannot be accepted,” said Ebtesam Al-Ketbi, of the Emirates Policy Center think tank, on Sunday. Shipping attacks A sign of growing unease about the prospect of renewed hostilities came last week when the GCC announced an advanced headquarters in Kuwait for its unified military command and the deployment of forces to the facility. The organization’s secretary general, Jasem Mohamed Al Budaiwi, said the move showed “a firm Gulf commitment to safeguarding the security and sovereignty of the GCC states” following what he called “heinous Iranian attacks.” Iran has also stepped up attacks on shipping in the Gulf, with almost daily claims – few of them substantiated – that tankers have struck mines as they’ve tried to transit the Strait of Hormuz. For Tehran, the increase in Gulf energy exports to close to pre-war levels in recent weeks, and the sharp decline in oil prices, deprive it of vital leverage in negotiations. The International Energy Agency said Gulf oil exports - excluding Oman - reached 18.4 million barrels a day in October, about 26% below prewar levels. At the same time, Iran has been unable to export any meaningful amount of its own crude for more than two months. The Iranian regime is demanding an end to the US blockade, the progressive removal of international sanctions and an unfreezing of billions of dollars in frozen assets as conditions for resuming negotiations with the US. But US President Donald Trump appears content to let the economic squeeze on Iran take its course, anticipating that Tehran will have to soften its terms and recognizing the Gulf states want to avoid another round of conflict. “At the request of the nations that I am ⁠looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly,” Trump said Thursday. At the same time, he canceled efforts by Vice President JD Vance to resurrect talks with Iran, declaring: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.” An unstable limbo Indeed, Iran’s economic pain appears to be deepening even as senior officials in Tehran insist it can withstand the pressure and can access hard currency to support the rial, whose value has fallen drastically since the conflict began. One perpetual sign of hardship is the long lines seen at gas stations in many parts of Iran. Esmail Saghab Esfahani, a vice president, admitted last week that there was a supply problem and that Iranians could no longer count on fuel stations to cover what they need. Some residents of the port city of Bandar Abbas blocked traffic on Thursday to protest against fuel shortages. The speaker of the Iranian parliament, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, suggested officials stop talking about the fuel issue, always sensitive in Iran. And yet there are no public indications the regime is ready to compromise. Baghaei was asked Sunday whether Iran would accept a temporary suspension of uranium enrichment or a reduction in enrichment levels in negotiations with Washington. “No. We are not at that stage at all. During this period, we are not discussing any details related to the nuclear issue, nor have we held any such discussions.” Ghalibaf said Sunday it made no difference whether Washington wanted negotiations or war. “If the Americans make another mistake this time, the capabilities and will of Iran’s armed forces will determine the geography of the battlefield.” Iran has frequently warned that another chapter in the conflict will see it broaden targets to infrastructure across the region, including subsea cables. Additionally, its Houthi allies in Yemen fire ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia almost daily and appear to have put Saudi-backed government forces under renewed pressure in the south of Yemen, forcing them to retreat from near the Red Sea in a setback in their campaign. The result is an unstable limbo across the region. “The United States may believe it can maintain the blockade for an extended period, but Iran sees it as a direct threat to its economy, sovereignty, and national security,” Israeli analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies, wrote on X. The US “cannot assume that time alone will force Tehran to surrender. Iran has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to absorb enormous economic costs rather than abandon what its leadership considers fundamental national interests.”

cnn.com.title: Israel kills senior Hamas commander in Gaza two months after killing his predecessor as ceasefire stagnates
cnn.com.text: Israel killed a senior Hamas commander involved in planning the October 7 attacks only two months after killing his predecessor, a fresh sign of how the Gaza conflict remains active despite a US-brokered ceasefire being in place. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) killed Samir Mahmoud Abu Younis, the commander of Hamas’ Rafah Brigade, in a strike in southern Gaza overnight Saturday, both Hamas and the IDF said. Abu Younis, who was a long-time member of the brigade, had replaced Nael Abu Obeid, the previous commander who was killed in a strike in September. And Abu Obeid himself replaced Mohammad Sabaneh, another commander of the Rafah Brigade who was killed in May 2025. The strike comes just days after an Israeli attack on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in what the IDF said was an attempt to kill another Hamas commander. In a statement, Hamas’ military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, acknowledged the death of Abu Younis, saying he had joined the brigade in 1991 and was “among the most prominent commanders who participated in planning and overseeing” the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. “The IDF continues to eliminate Hamas leaders in Gaza, and another one joins his predecessors in the depths of hell,” said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. “The offensive policy that I am leading together with the Prime Minister and the IDF in Gaza will continue – until Gaza is demilitarized and there is no Hamas.” The killing of Abu Younis underscores an emerging pattern in Gaza. Despite a nominal ceasefire that went into effect more than one year ago, Israel has continued to carry out strikes targeting members of Hamas, particularly senior commanders. But those commanders are quickly replaced as Hamas entrenches its own grip on power over the half of Gaza not occupied by Israel. Meanwhile, the Board of Peace, a body created by the Trump administration with United Nations backing to oversee the Gaza ceasefire plan, remains sidelined, unable to make any substantive progress on the 20-point plan agreed to in October 2025. On Friday, the board said it had held “very constructive discussions” with 17 countries about a civilian Gaza police force under the authority of a Palestinian technocratic committee that was supposed to run Gaza. But that committee has yet to enter the enclave, and an international security force meant to stabilize Gaza has yet to materialize. The IDF strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza last week killed at least six people, including a doctor and a child, according to Palestinian officials. The strike hit the hospital’s surgery unit, killing Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira and a 13-year-old boy who was awaiting surgery. A total of 40 others were injured in the strike, including two doctors who were in critical condition, officials said. In a statement, the IDF said it had targeted the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade, Muhammad Abu Ismail, as well as “additional terrorists who were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.” But when pressed on whether Abu Ismail was killed in the strike, the IDF did not answer. Doctors Without Borders (Médicins Sans Frontières, or MSF) condemned the strike, saying: “It is unconscionable that patients and medical staff are once again being killed and injured inside a hospital, a place where lives should be saved, not taken.” MSF withdrew its own staff from the hospital in January because of the presence of armed men inside, as well as concerns over the hospital’s neutrality and management. “Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected,” MSF said. The Board of Peace also urged both Israel and Hamas to uphold their commitments under the Comprehensive Peace Plan and protect civilians. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 people have been killed in near-daily Israeli strikes in Gaza since the ceasefire was signed one year ago. The shattered territory also faces an unfolding humanitarian crisis ahead of the onset of winter. Last week, seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, where nearly two million Palestinians remain displaced. In a joint statement Sunday, the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom said 150,000 tents and other vital supplies were being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza. They urged Israel to allow “immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access” and permit tents and dual-use items needed for humanitarian operations and early recovery into the enclave. Israel said last week that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead of winter, but it has refused to allow in the heavy equipment needed for large-scale clean-up and rubble removal efforts. “The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms,” said Israel’s Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories.

cnn.com.title: As students rely on AI in college applications, admissions offices scramble to keep up
cnn.com.text: The college admissions essay is in a very weird place. It’s impossible to say just how many of them are now written by AI, but at this point, experts agree that it’s a lot of them. And while colleges generally frown upon that practice, they’re using AI to evaluate the essays, too. It’s all adding up to a scramble to stay ahead over the future of who gets to go to the university of their choice. Kate Gilbertson, who graduated from UC Berkeley in 2025 and edits college applications full time, said that lately she’s received a lot of drafts that don’t have the usual quirks of teenage writing. “Those little moments of flaw tell me that this is still a 17-year-old’s writing, right?” Gilbertson said. It’s not just essays. Though ChatGPT has been out for just four years, AI has already reshaped the entire college admissions process from top to bottom. Now, as the January 1 deadline for the Common App approaches, more and more high schoolers are using AI in their college applications and even turning to chatbots instead of college counselors, who often charge thousands of dollars for their services. Meanwhile, colleges are rushing to update their AI usage guidelines and rethink the future of the essay. Yet they are also testing out AI evaluations of their own to help sift through thousands, if not tens of thousands, of applications. Students, meanwhile, see an obvious double standard: If some universities are using AI to grade essays, why can’t I? If everyone is using AI to get ahead, why should I get left behind? Different rules for different schools Admissions offices around the country are rushing to figure out guidelines for AI use in applications, and each one looks a little bit different. But “students are moving faster than admissions offices” when it comes to AI, Ashley Pallie, California Institute of Technology’s dean of undergraduate admissions, said. CalTech, which is at the forefront of AI research, takes a nuanced approach. Its admissions office whittled down thousands of applicants to less than 450 admitted students last year. For Pallie, the process is much more art than science. She said an AI bot couldn’t replace the job of professional essay readers anytime soon. While “replacing your unique voice and tone with AI generated content” is unethical, the school said that “generating questions or exercises to help kick start the brainstorming process” is okay. The University of Pennsylvania warned against AI usage for letters of recommendation written by counselors and teachers. Colleges are also differing in how they grade essays, with some using AI tools themselves. “You actually can’t develop the perfect formula that’s going to choose the right students for you. You do need humans who are reading the humans who submitted their application,” Pallie said. However, CalTech does use an AI that reads students’ scientific research and asks them questions that faculty later views. Major public universities like Virginia Tech, which received a record 57,6222 first-year applications for 2025, are testing out AI to keep up with the mass application volume. That experimentation hasn’t always worked. UNC-Chapel Hill reversed its decision to auto-score application essays based on writing quality. The student newspaper reported that a university spokesperson said that “the widespread use of AI-assisted writing tools was the factor diminishing the usefulness of AI essay ratings.” Is this the end of the college essay? More colleges are dropping supplemental essays altogether for this application cycle. Tulane said that it is no longer requiring a “Why Tulane?” essay. While spokesperson Michael Strecker told CNN the essay hasn’t been that important in the selection process in recent years, he “can confirm that concerns about AI did play a role in this decision.” Sophie Sajnani, who graduated college in 2025, founded a boutique college consulting firm. Sajnani discourages her students from using AI to help brainstorm, but doesn’t mind when it writes for them. When asked if there’s a concern that all the essays will sound the same, she said her students are AI-native and have trained their AI chatbots to sound like them. And she said there’s been a spike in enrollment in her firm’s AI literacy program. “The reason we still have the admissions essay is to show a moment of growth. I think it’s less so about the writing and more so to show situations and how a student has grown from it,” Sajnani said. Some students aren’t totally sold on AI writing, but see its benefits for other parts of the admissions process. “I feel like when using AI, people want to think that you want to cheat the process,” Anisah Ali, a high school junior in Washington, told CNN. “I see it more as you want to open up ideas in your brain that you wouldn’t think about doing yourself.” Pallie does see a distant future where college essays don’t play as big a role. But, in a way, the replacement is even more person-facing than the essay. “In our ideal world, everyone would do an interview of some sort,” Pallie said. But the style of that interview? “Human.” But not all uses of AI in the college application process are as controversial. Leveling the playing field The college admissions process begins with deciding which schools are the best fit. In this case, AI can help students who are putting together applications on their own or whose families can’t afford to spend thousands on private college consultants. This year, ChatGPT launched a college planner for teens. OpenAI said the most popular prompts included “ask questions to develop my ideas,” “give feedback on my draft” and “help me check my evidence.” “For a lot of students, AI is the college counselor they can’t afford,” Michael Koppenheffer, chief innovation officer of enrollment solutions at EAB, told CNN. “They can get more information and they get more detailed guidance than they ever could before.” EAB found that AI plays the an outsized role in influencing what schools students applied to, compared to resources like college’s websites and search. Eighty-two percent of students surveyed in its AI report said they used ChatGPT when asked what AI tools they used in their college search. Christine Wilson, who already utilizes AI to help run her marketing agency in Virginia, at first hired a college counselor for her son, Ronan, who “built a list for him of initial schools that then we ended up kind of redoing ourselves using AI.” She used Claude to make a spreadsheet of the 22 universities Ronan applied to last year. The spreadsheet ran an analysis of the cost of attendance for each school, taking stats like income and potential aid into account. It saved Wilson “many, many hours of research,” she said. Wilson and her son ran a separate analysis for colleges that had football, Greek life and prestigious business schools. (Ronan ended up committing to The University of Florida.) Bunmi Emenanjo’s 17-year-old daughter has specific criteria for her future university: It has to be urban, offer merit aid and have a diverse student body. While she hired a college counselor for her older son, this year they are relying on Claude. “It’s just easier to use AI to search for that versus going through each school and digging up that information,” Emenanjo said. But for her family, the application itself will use more of the traditional methods – she said her daughter won’t be using AI for her essays.

cnn.com.title: Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace from Nvidia. Many in Silicon Valley are still showering him with support
cnn.com.text: Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia was marked by corporate scandal, but many of his own former employees and colleagues across Silicon Valley are coming out in droves to express support for the man they believe to be a legend. Huang resigned on Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with at least one subordinate. He had already been under scrutiny after reports of an affair with another woman, who was described by US officials as a potential Chinese intelligence asset. Huang was so integral to Nvidia’s brand that his image — with signature black leather jacket — was often turned into marketing material, including an AI-powered hologram at the company’s annual conference, known as GTC. Known for its low turnover and flat corporate structure, with Huang managing over 50 direct reports and responding to messages at all hours, Nvidia fostered deep employee loyalty. Following his departure, current and former staff responded with tributes on social media. Edward Liu, a director and distinguished scientist who started as an intern at the company, called it “a heartbreaking day,” in a post on X, praising Huang as an inspiring leader who taught them to “reason from first principles.” Engineer Fei Peng went even further, writing that Huang’s departure “has killed NVIDIA’s soul.” Others, like senior research scientist Gavin Woolery, openly suggested ulterior motives and suspicions about his ousting. Woolery posted on X that he felt Huang’s ousting came too quickly before all the information emerged. “Everyone deserves a fair trial. It’s possible he has made mistakes, I’m not sure they were ill-intentioned ones, but in either case we should know the whole truth before we judge,” Woolery said. Other employees expressed support for Nvidia’s interim leader, CFO Colette Kress. “I am grief-stricken that Jensen is no longer with NVIDIA,” posted Bryan Catanzaro, Nvidia’s vice president of applied deep learning research. “At the same time, I fully support NVIDIA’s board and have confidence in their decisions. I’ve worked with Colette for years and know her as an extraordinary leader. She has my full support.” Beyond Nvidia’s walls, Huang’s influence was felt across the broader tech ecosystem. Often called the “central bank” of the booming AI industry, Nvidia not only supplied the hardware powering the technology but also financed much of the sector through investments and partnerships, with Huang serving as its biggest cheerleader. That has led to criticism and fears of “circular financing,” in which Nvidia invests in companies that fuel its own growth when those businesses turn around and use Nvidia capital to purchase Nvidia products. Exolabs founder Alex Cheema wrote about cold emailing Huang in June about an idea to make local AI much faster on Nvidia hardware. Huang responded in seven minutes and “approved a war room for us to work on this at NVIDIA HQ,” Cheema wrote. Cheema pointed to Huang’s long-time support and promotion of open-source technology — software or hardware built on publicly accessible source code that anyone can freely inspect, modify and distribute. Most of the major AI models, like ChatGPT and Claude, run on closed-source systems. “I don’t believe Jensen is replaceable, he’s a 1 of 1 human, but I hope NVIDIA will continue to aggressively support Open Source AI and Local AI, and continue to take bets on small startups with crazy ideas,” Cheema said. Huang also found support among his peers — some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley and venture capital, including his longtime friend and business partner, Elon Musk. Even before Huang was ousted, Musk posted that it would be “an honor” to hire Huang after another user on X implored him to do so. “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk later posted on Friday after Huang’s resignation. “Dark, dark day. Horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world,” Andreessen Horowitz general partner Martin Casado posted on X. The firm’s account also posted a clip from a movie about Michael Jordan, along with the quote: “ You’re gonna be remembered forever because some things are eternal.” Even those who have criticized his actions, like Sequoia Capital’s Shaun MaGuire, who called Huang’s actions a “dumb mistake” and “bad for America,” often come with a dose of praise. “He made huge mistakes with his infidelity, which is tragic for his family and NVDA. But simultaneously he will leave a huge void, with the loss of a: technical, aggressive, founder-CEO,” MaGuire wrote on X.

cnn.com.title: Trump sank the GOP in 2026. He could do it again in 2028
cnn.com.text: Judging by their choices since this month’s Democratic sweep, both the White House and congressional Republicans are vastly underestimating the party’s risk in 2028 if President Donald Trump remains as unpopular as he is now. Dazed Republicans picking through the wreckage of their losses may console themselves with the thought that Trump’s dire approval ratings won’t pose as large a threat to the GOP in 2028, since he will be leaving the White House. But history strongly suggests that confidence is misplaced. Outgoing presidents have cast a larger shadow than even many political professionals assume in the election to succeed them — especially when that retiring president faces widespread public discontent, as Trump does now. While popular outgoing presidents haven’t always ensured victory for their designated successors, the inverse has almost always been true: When the outgoing president is unpopular, his party has rarely won the election to replace him. This month’s election underscored the danger looming for Republicans if Trump remains this weak. In House, Senate and gubernatorial elections across the country, the vast majority of voters who disapproved of Trump’s job performance — usually at least 80% of them — voted against Republican candidates, according to the most recently updated numbers as of November 12 from the Voter Polls conducted for CNN and other media organizations by SRSS. “This massive repudiation of Republican candidates is totally and completely about Donald Trump,” said longtime GOP pollster Whit Ayres. Even big losses in a midterm don’t guarantee defeat for the party holding the White House in the next presidential election. But presidents who have recovered from a bad midterm have usually changed direction in response to the rebuke (like Harry Truman after 1946 or Bill Clinton after 1994) or benefited from changing circumstances (as Ronald Reagan did when the economy recovered after his party’s poor 1982 midterm). Trump, by contrast, remains caught in a grinding war against Iran with no clear exit. And far from adjusting his course, he has reaffirmed it with the appointment of Stephen Miller, his most ideologically extreme senior adviser, as White House chief of staff. House Republicans have responded to their losses in a similar way by choosing pugnacious Rep. Jim Jordan as their new leader. “Donald Trump is going to double down and triple down” on the policies and style that alienated voters this year, said Steve Schmidt, a longtime GOP strategist who has become a staunch Trump critic. “Any person with any attachment to real life would look at this election and say, ‘Well, they certainly should have gotten the message and they’ll be chastened,’ but that doesn’t appreciate the physics of politics, which is that as an extreme party gets smaller, it becomes more fanatical.” History is clear on the consequences Novelist Leo Tolstoy famously wrote that every happy family is alike, while every unhappy family is different. The relationship of outgoing presidents to the election to succeed them inverts that maxim: The impact of every unsuccessful president has been largely the same, while the role of successful presidents has diverged. Good feelings toward popular retiring presidents Theodore Roosevelt in 1908 and Ronald Reagan in 1988 helped each man’s designated successor win election. But despite very strong job approval ratings, both Dwight Eisenhower in 1960 and Bill Clinton in 2000 saw their vice-presidents lose nail biters (although Al Gore, Clinton’s No. 2, did win the popular vote). Barack Obama in 2016 wasn’t as popular as Eisenhower or Clinton, but he also left office with majority approval — only to see his party’s designated heir, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, lose another tight race to Trump (despite, like Gore, winning the popular vote). But when an outgoing president has lost the public’s support, the record is far more consistent. Since the turn of the 20th century, each time an outgoing president has been broadly unpopular, his party has lost the race to succeed him. That was true for Democrats Woodrow Wilson in 1920, Harry Truman in 1952, Lyndon Johnson in 1968 and Biden in 2024, as well as for Republican George W. Bush in 2008. According to the exit polls conducted for CNN and other media organizations, 88% of the voters who disapproved of Reagan in 1988 and Clinton in 2000 voted for the other party’s presidential candidate. In 2016, 89% of voters who disapproved of Obama voted for Trump; in 2024, 82% of voters who disapproved of Biden voted for Trump over Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump’s two victories help explain why a popular outgoing president is no guarantee of success for his party — while an unpopular retiring president has been a more reliable kiss of death. In 2016, according to the exit polls, Obama’s approval remained at or just above 50% in each of six swing states he had won in 2012. But Trump still flipped all of them — Iowa, Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Florida. The reason is that Trump captured a significantly larger share among the minority of voters who disapproved of Obama than Clinton won among the majority who approved. Trump harnessed virtually all the discontent about Obama, while Clinton’s own vulnerabilities prevented her from capturing as much of his support. In 2024, the equation for Harris proved much more straightforward — and treacherous. Between 56% to 60% of voters in the seven major swing states disapproved of Biden’s performance and between 81% to 87% of those disapprovers backed Trump, powering him to victory in all of them, the exit polls found. Harris made missteps as a candidate, but her biggest problem was that pervasive discontent with the administration in which she served. In recent times, the presidential nominee who had the most success separating from an unpopular outgoing president of his own party was Republican Sen. John McCain in 2008. Running against Obama, McCain won 30% of voters nationwide who disapproved of George W. Bush, the exit polls found. As a senator who had occasionally clashed with Bush — and ran a bitter race against him for the GOP nomination in 2000 — McCain wasn’t intrinsically tied to his predecessor as closely as Harris, Gore and George H.W. Bush (who all served as vice presidents to the retiring president) or Hillary Clinton, who worked as Obama’s secretary of state. “There were famously enmities there,” between McCain and Bush, noted Schmidt, McCain’s chief strategist in the 2008 race. Yet Schmidt said the campaign recognized it would take dramatic, even unprecedented, actions to overcome the public’s disapproval of Bush — which reached a stunning 71% in the 2008 exit poll amid fatigue with the Iraq War and fear and anger over that year’s financial crisis. “It drove everything as a political consideration because you knew that there was a day of reckoning where you had to disrupt that headwind and fly out of it,” Schmidt said. That impulse, he said, drove McCain’s attempt to name Democrat-turned independent Sen. Joe Lieberman as his running mate. “It was going to take something like that to arrest the trajectory,” Schmidt recalled. (When Republicans rebelled over Lieberman, McCain abruptly pivoted to choosing Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin instead.) In the end, even McCain could not paddle nearly fast enough to escape the undertow of Bush’s capsizing presidency. Obama that year won a higher share of the popular vote than any Democratic nominee since Johnson in 1964 and flipped nine states that had voted for Bush in 2004. In all of them, at least two-thirds of voters disapproved of Bush’s performance — and at least two-thirds of those disapprovers backed Obama. The GOP’s 2028 conundrum Through 2026, the one discordant sign for Democrats was polling consistently showing they were not winning nearly as many voters who disapproved of Trump as during his first term. Democrats this year didn’t fully match the benchmarks they hit among Trump disapprovers in his first term. But ultimately Democrats carried about the same share of voters who disapproved of Trump as the opposition party did among voters who disapproved of Obama in 2010, Bush in 2006 and Bill Clinton in 1994. In the 2026 CNN Voter Poll measuring preferences in the national House popular vote, 86% of voters who disapproved of Trump backed Democrats; the party also won 85% to 89% of voters who disapproved of Trump in almost all the major Senate contests. That was plenty to power a Democratic landslide. Disapproval of Trump in this election was not only deep (at 63%, his national disapproval rating was considerably higher than those other presidents in their worst midterm elections), but also broad. Across the 45 states where Voter Poll data is available, most voters approved of Trump’s job performance in only five sparsely populated deep-red states — Arkansas, Idaho, South Dakota, West Virginia, and Wyoming. In every state where Democrats flipped a governorship, a Senate seat, or both, a substantial majority of voters disapproved of Trump’s job performance — and those disenchanted voters provided the core of the winning Democratic coalition. In Texas, for instance, 96% of the votes for Democratic Senate victor James Talarico came from people who disapproved of Trump. One reason Republicans could not surmount the Trump discontent in 2028 was that so few displayed any independence from him. As Ayres noted, Republicans concluded that if they clashed with Trump, he would either hound them out of the party or defeat them in primaries. Yet binding themselves to Trump to avoid primary challenges created insurmountable problems in the general election where “Trump and Trumpism have become toxic,” Ayres said. That same conundrum looms over the potential 2028 Republican presidential field, particularly Vice President JD Vance. Trump is likely to fire social media thunderbolts against any attempt from Vance or other candidates to meaningfully distance from him, and no one seeking the nomination can afford too much conflict with the president, given his durable popularity with the MAGA base. Yet if Trump remains anywhere near as unpopular with the broad public as he is today, failing to separate from him could prove fatal for the eventual GOP nominee in the general election. Vance himself seems to be aware of this catch-22; CNN reported last week that the vice president has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028 in the wake of the GOP’s disastrous midterm performance. There’s little sign Republicans will change course All this underscores the GOP’s stake in Trump mounting at least some recovery by 2028. A decisive conclusion to the Iran War that lowered gas and diesel prices might lift him somewhat. But Democratic pollster Anna Greenberg said it will be extremely difficult for Trump to regain much of the allegiance he lost over the past two years among the new voters who moved toward him in 2024 — particularly Hispanic Americans, Black men and younger men. Most of those voters, she said, feel not only disappointed but angry at Trump for failing to alleviate their economic squeeze as he promised — while focusing so much on his own priorities, like building monuments and padding his fortune. “Especially for the people who are less ideologically committed to him… the betrayal and the broken promises make it very hard to come back from,” Greenberg said. “It’s not just the bad job performance.” As problematic, Trump and congressional Republicans show no sign of rethinking the course that ran the party into this electoral ditch. Instead, through the elevation of the belligerent hard-liners Miller and Jordan, the GOP has not only ignored but actively rejected the voters’ roar of discontent. Add the prospect of extensive congressional hearings exposing corruption and self-dealing in the administration and many analysts believe Trump’s approval rating could fall even lower by 2028. “He may not be at his lowest point,” saud Emory University political scientist Alan Abramowitz, who has extensively studied the relationship between election outcomes and presidential approval. “He is going to have a hard time clawing his way back up to anything higher than he is now, given what is likely to be happening” with investigations and the economy. If Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio wins the GOP nomination in 2028, they might find it especially difficult to escape negative feelings about Trump, since they served so closely with him. But, as Abramowitz said, “every prominent Republican has tied themselves closely to Trump over the past two years.” Though voters still harbor many doubts about Democrats, if Trump can’t repair his public standing, those Democratic vulnerabilities may not matter as much as Republicans hope — just as they did little to stop the massive blue tide earlier this month.

cnn.com.title: Democrats look to what’s next after Trump. But first, an actual party
cnn.com.text: The Democrats here were told: The big midterm win wasn’t about you. But the vibes among the hundreds of party operatives, strategists and would-be 2028 presidential candidates who gathered to ask what’s next after nearly a decade of living in President Donald Trump’s shadow? Party on, Wayne! Party on, Garth! Democrats arguably haven’t had such a wide-open presidential field since the “Wayne’s World” era, when a preternaturally talented Southern state governor named Bill Clinton came almost out of nowhere to win the White House in 1992. Now, Democrats have exploded out of a Trump-imposed political wilderness to their most sweeping midterm win since Watergate. And they were ready to take a beat before they begin what’s sure to be a frenzied season of presidential campaign announcements, hiring, fundraising and knife-fighting among a dozen or more White House hopefuls. Even the would-be candidates could barely hide their elation during donor dinners, at hotel rooftop receptions, and over drinks at the bar at the Ritz-Carlton in downtown Denver, where many mingled late into the night. But on the main stage, on the first day, those gathered here were warned: Voters still aren’t all that into them. “These voters that we lost and that we have turned away are still out there and they have not become Democrats yet,” influential Democratic data guru David Shor said as the two-day gathering kicked off. “They will be here in two years, and if we have not persuaded them by then, we might not be happy with how things turn out.” There was no agreement about how to do that. The prescriptions coming from the stage previewed the struggle that’s beginning to emerge: Did Tuesday’s wins signal an uncompromising fighter from the party’s left wing can dominate the nominating contest and go on to win a national election? Or is the message that to win everywhere, the party should choose someone who can appeal to the voters who rejected the woke culture-war politics of the Covid era? “The American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump,” said Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. “The only way we’re going to fix that is by fixing it together. We can’t do it with the same warfare that brought us here,” said Rob Sand, the incoming Democratic governor of Iowa. Contrast those two millennial red-state newcomers with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, who hails from deep-blue California, co-chaired Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign in 2020, and is widely expected to run for president in 2028 as an unapologetic progressive. “This is not the 1990s. We cannot cobble together a fleeting big tent through perpetual triangulating, straddling, and calculating,” Khanna said onstage. The reference to “triangulating” was an unmistakable jab at a buzzword of the Clinton era. The gathering offered a few reminders of the anger emanating from the party’s base. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen spoke after announcing he would challenge Chuck Schumer to be the next Senate majority leader. Likely incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries was heckled by the audience, with one person yelling Jeffries was “a f**king liar!” before being escorted from the hall. And protesters gathered outside the security perimeter, holding signs that read, “Abolish billionaires,” “No Schumer coronation,” and “No more do-nothing Democrats.” A Denver SWAT vehicle was parked between them and the rideshare dropoff line. But inside that perimeter and off the stage, all the divisions evaporated into an atmosphere of celebration bordering on elation. There were food trucks parked outside the brewery serving local craft beers on draft. There were musical acts performing in the outdoor plaza in between speeches. Both days were about 65 degrees and sunny, with the weather clear enough to see the mountains. And it was very cozy and comfortable after hours at at the Ritz bar. The drinks started flowing Thursday night, with Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, who’s considering a presidential run, holding court. Pete Buttigieg was also spotted there Thursday night, as was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. And Friday evening, the nationwide FAA ground stop stranded everyone in Denver at least for a few hours. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin sat with Govs. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherill of New Jersey until the stop was lifted. Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock huddled off the record with reporters. Buttigieg was back too, spotted snapping a selfie or two. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker couldn’t attend the conference, but his team was at the Ritz bar too. So were operatives with ties to Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and a handful of others. This was where the conference’s real business unfolded. A top priority was recruiting staff and making connections for presidential campaigns that are set to start kicking off as soon as January, if not earlier, according to conversations with over a dozen strategists and operatives with ties to presidential hopefuls. Much of the chatter and speculation focused on possible candidates who weren’t in the room, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez chief among them. Their decisions to run or not to run for president in 2028 will fundamentally shape the rest of the field. Wins across the South underscore the power of Black voters, already perhaps the most important single constituency in any Democratic primary, and Harris starts with an enormous advantage there, especially among Black women. And then there’s the progressive wing, energized by victories from working-class candidates and people like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. “People are thinking there’s more room for someone on the left, and wondering if it means AOC is going to run,” said one top operative with close ties to a likely 2028 Democratic presidential candidate. There was also widespread speculation about Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, whose been widely considered a top-tier likely 2028 contender. At the heart of his appeal had been the argument he can win big in one of the most important swing states on the map. Now, he’s got a lot of competition from newer faces in the party. “I’m proud to be the governor of what I think is the swingiest state in America, but we got a lot of company now,” Shapiro told me in an interview. “Look at Texas, look at South Carolina, Iowa, and a whole lot more. But I think that presents an opportunity for Democrats not to be thinking about how to get to 270 on an electoral map, but get to 370 back how Obama won and Clinton won.” Other potential contenders, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, also didn’t appear here. Newsom, who had occupied something of frontrunner status in the invisible primary as he jabbed at Trump over the past year, seemed to have faded somewhat from the main conversation, at least in these halls. (Newsom hasn’t faded, apparently, for Trump, who spent part of his weekend attacking Newsom for commuting the death sentences of all California inmates on death row and changing them to life without parole.) As the hundreds of Democrats who gathered here struggled to find a way out of Denver, the airport chaos almost presaged what could be a massive post-Trump hangover for a party that’s elated but set for a bruising internal struggle over what’s next. “If you ask the American people, there is no question about who we oppose,” said Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss. “But also no sense of what we believe. That is the question we have to answer right now.”

cnn.com.title: Lutnick under fire: How Trump’s commerce secretary cultivated Nvidia’s CEO while chip controls slipped
cnn.com.text: The first call, as Jensen Huang remembers it, came from Howard Lutnick. It was around the start of Donald Trump’s second term, and Lutnick was preparing to become his Commerce Secretary. His message to the head of Nvidia was simple: whenever you need the president, call us. Recounting the call on Joe Rogan’s podcast last December, Huang remembered fondly that Lutnick had called him and his company “a national treasure.” Two years later, Huang has resigned from Nvidia and Lutnick is under intense scrutiny for what some Trump advisers see as inaction in placing limits on US chip exports to China and his role in cultivating Huang as a top administration ally. Other administration officials have accused Lutnick of bucking internal consensus and Trump’s own directives in failing to blacklist an Nvidia customer suspected of funneling chips to China. Some of Trump’s advisers, reeling from the fallout of Huang’s resignation, have begun discussing whether Lutnick should be dismissed, according to people familiar with the conversations. This account is derived from more than a dozen sources, including officials inside the administration and the tech industry. They described a rapidly deepening relationship that came to influence nearly all areas of the White House’s stance toward some of the most powerful technology in the world. Questions surrounding the scandal — and the fresh push to limit sales of advanced chips to China — are likely to persist as Trump prepares to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, the hub of China’s tech industry. American officials said they didn’t expect Trump to raise the alleged spying with Xi, and said China wouldn’t have a say in whether Washington tightens restrictions on access to chips. ‘What the hell is Nvidia?’ Until shortly after Trump’s inauguration last year, Huang was nearly a stranger to Trump’s world. He would skip the swearing-in to spend Lunar New Year with employees in Asia, while his tech titan counterparts Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos had prime spots in the Capitol Rotunda. Trump, by his own account, had barely heard of Nvidia or its CEO: “What’s his name? What the hell is Nvidia?” he recalled wondering a few months later. “I’ve never heard of it before.” His ignorance wouldn’t last long. Eleven days after being sworn in for a second term, Trump met Huang at the White House. Huang also met that day with Lutnick, still awaiting confirmation as Commerce Secretary. As Trump signed executive orders in the Oval Office later that afternoon with the cameras rolling, he was full of praise for the man he’d only recently met. “He’s a great gentleman, and I hadn’t met him,” Trump said as he reflected on what he called a good meeting. “He’s the biggest in the world in terms of chips.” Over the next two years, the relationship would deepen over dinners, phone calls and many, many meetings. It was aided at every step by Lutnick, who helped elevate Huang’s profile and whose agency is responsible for keeping sensitive American technology away from adversaries. On Thursday, after Huang resigned from Nvidia following revelations he had extramarital affairs with two women, one of whom may be connected to China, Lutnick’s critics began circling. Administration officials who have long been concerned about Huang’s influence on Trump said privately that the Commerce Department failed to crack down on chip shipments to companies suspected of passing them on secretly to China. Speaking on CNBC Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a wide swath of Trump’s administration — including the Treasury and State departments, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative — favored placing the company at the center of the scandal, Megaspeed, on an export blacklist. He said it was the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, that had failed to follow through. “Commerce…has the pen…and you will have to ask them about their internal process,” he said. Both Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill demanded Lutnick answer questions about what he knew, and when. House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats wrote to Lutnick demanding to know what he and his export control chief, Jeffrey Kessler, knew about Megaspeed, and when. Senate Democrats directed Lutnick to preserve documents, communications and records related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced chips. And some Democrats went further in their criticism of Lutnick. “I think he should be fired,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen told ABC News in an interview that aired Sunday. Van Hollen, the top Democrat on the Senate subcommittee that oversees Commerce Department funding, is running to be Senate majority leader in the next Congress. “This news is as concerning as it gets,” Sen. Jim Banks, a Trump ally, said Thursday on Fox News. “When you’re in a war with another country, you don’t give them your best technologies. And that’s why lawmakers, for the last two years, have been pushing hard to stop our high-end computer chips from being exported to China.” The White House said Thursday Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” Lutnick was expected to join Trump on a trip to China next week, and officials have not indicated those plans have changed amid the Nvidia scandal. A deepening relationship A few months after Huang’s first Oval Office meeting, Lutnick played a role in facilitating Huang’s attendance at a $1-million-a-head MAGA Inc. dinner at Mar-a-Lago, according to two people familiar with the matter. The April dinner proved fateful. Huang used it to make a final appeal against planned restrictions on selling Nvidia’s H20 chip to Chinese customers. Trump, meanwhile, walked away impressed with his new, extraordinarily wealthy friend. Huang’s charm offensive at the Palm Beach dinner seemed to work, but only briefly. The White House moved to shelve the planned curbs. But as a trade war with China heated up, Nvidia later disclosed that the government had told it that H20 sales to China would require a license – and that the requirement would stay in place indefinitely. Huang kept working at it. At an Investing in America event at the end of April 2025, Lutnick and Huang were photographed together in the Cross Hall. Trump turned the moment into a show of affection. “I could have Jensen negotiating. He’d blow my people away,” Trump said. “Even Howard would say that.” Lutnick, sitting in the audience, quickly concurred. “We’ll take him.” By July, Huang was back in the Oval Office. His pitch this time was tailored to Trump. Selling chips to China, he argued, could create American jobs and cement American AI as the world standard. He had already said publicly in May that the ban already cost Nvidia $15 billion in sales. Two top administration officials who had become close Huang allies accompanied him in the Oval Office: Lutnick and David Sacks, the White House AI adviser, who championed “exporting the US AI stack” – the idea that selling older chips like the H20 abroad keeps the world hooked on American technology. Five days later, Nvidia announced the government had assured it that it would be permitted to sell the H20 in China. Huang was in Beijing when he said sales would resume. The next day, Lutnick went on CNBC, explaining the decision as a way to get China “addicted to the American technology stack.” The H20 deal was finished in August, and the president negotiated it himself, directly with Huang, as they sat face-to-face in the White House. Lutnick’s agency immediately moved to issue H20 licenses. Trump would go on to publicly confirm the arrangement that made the H20 sales possible: Nvidia would pay the government 15% of its China chip revenue. Through the fall, Huang drew closer to the president, and Trump regularly mentioned Huang off-the-cuff in his public remarks. In October, Trump spoke with Huang, Marc Benioff and other business leaders about sending federal law enforcement into San Francisco, and the next day he called the plan off, citing those conversations. That same month, as Trump was preparing to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in South Korea, Nvidia donated $25 million to Trump’s White House ballroom project, a person familiar with the matter said. Nvidia never appeared on the published donor list. The warnings In the summer of 2025, as Trump and Huang were growing closer, a phone call began to unravel something larger. Singapore police, investigating a cloud company called Megaspeed, questioned its former managing director, Alice Huang, and barred her from leaving the country. She had met Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in California in early 2024. The two were photographed together at a trade show in Taipei that June. During a briefing with lawmakers on Capitol Hill at the end of 2025, federal agents said they suspected Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” citing his close relationship with Alice Huang, according to sources familiar with the meeting. The briefing was centered on an investigation into suspected efforts to circumvent US export control restrictions and attempts to influence the Trump administration’s policy on shipping certain Nvidia chips to China, according to the sources. The FBI, which is conducting the primary counterintelligence investigation, told lawmakers last year that it was particularly suspicious of Alice Huang’s seemingly overnight career pivot from Chinese State television journalist to businesswoman with an unusually large amount of purchasing power in the Chinese economy, one of the sources said. Trump himself had been briefed on intelligence about Alice Huang in late 2025 and took no action, CNN previously reported. But the investigations continued. The Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 to determine whether the firm had run afoul of US export rules, but had stopped short of placing the company on the so-called Entity List, a trade blacklist that bars US suppliers from selling to listed firms without a license. Other areas of the administration had grown frustrated at the delay, including at the State Department and National Security Council, people familiar with the matter said. On Capitol Hill, Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, had taken notice and quickly fired off a direct request to Lutnick to investigate Megaspeed. Behind the scenes, executive branch officials from other national security agencies were raising Megaspeed as a clear target for investigation and inclusion on Commerce’s Entity List. They got no substantive response. And in meetings when the case came up, Lutnick’s deputies would respond by telling officials little more than it was Lutnick’s decision to make, according to people familiar with the conversations. In the CNBC interview Friday, Bessent suggested the inaction had violated directives given by Trump himself. “I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” Bessent said, referring to an older-generation data-center chip. “And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage.” When Trump was preparing to travel to China for a state visit in May, the delegation announced on May 11 initially didn’t include Huang. The next day, Trump phoned Huang to invite him. As Trump flew aboard Air Force One to Anchorage that afternoon with Elon Musk and Sean Hannity, he received a briefing from Secretary of State Marco Rubio about some of the concerns surrounding Huang and China. On the ground in Alaska, Huang boarded for the final leg to Beijing. On May 14, Xi greeted Trump at the Great Hall of the People, and Musk, Huang and Apple’s Tim Cook were the only executives the White House listed at the arrival ceremony. Huang called it “one of the most important summits in human history.” In the months that followed, there was little to indicate Trump or Lutnick had concerns about Huang. Trump praised him in the Oval Office. Lutnick, moderating a September G20 session in North Carolina, called him “an American treasure” — the same flattery deployed on their first phone call nearly two years earlier. In September, Huang took a call from Trump on stage and put him on speakerphone at a summit in Los Angeles. Trump called AI-takeover fears “a hoax,” called data centers “the oil of the next 20, 25 years,” and said opposition played into China’s hands. Ten days later, Huang and his wife were at the White House to attend Trump’s State Dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping. They were seated at the head table with the two leaders and their spouses. The reckoning Less than a month later, the first bombshell dropped: US officials had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who had cultivated a close relationship with Jensen Huang. CNN later reported the US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between Alice Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing. Trump, officials said, would not hang his friend out to dry. As one official put it, Huang’s problems were Nvidia’s, Nvidia’s were the economy’s, and that became the president’s problem. Trump called Huang “brilliant” and, “unless we find out something to the contrary,” “very above board.” But the political ground had also shifted. Democrats won both chambers in the midterm elections, and voters rejected data-center projects in 40 of 41 ballot measures. The Republican chairs of three House committees – Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and the China select committee, all set to lose their gavels in January – asked Huang as well as Nvidia’s general counsel for closed-door interviews next month. Kessler, Lutnick’s deputy at the Commerce Department, has also been asked to appear at a hearing scheduled for next month. Republicans are now accusing Lutnick of putting Trump in a vulnerable position. “Shame on Lutnick for allowing that exposure to happen for the president. Raises a question about what other ones are out there,” Sen. Thom Tillis told reporters Thursday. During a meeting in the Situation Room last week, Treasury Secretary Bessent turned to Lutnick and asked why Megaspeed wasn’t on the entities list. According to sources familiar with the meeting, Lutnick stammered, “I don’t know. I’ll look into it.” This article has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: The systems used to keep America flying are ancient. That makes fixing the problem that much more difficult
cnn.com.text: In some ways, America’s air traffic control system performs far better than one might think — even if it would be tough to convince the more than one million passengers who had their travel plans upended in recent days. It handles a huge airspace and more than 45,000 flights a day. Yet, failures are exceedingly rare, even when its antiquated equipment breaks down. The current system uses strips of paper with the names of flights on them to be handed off from one controller to another, floppy computer discs and copper wire to handle communications for nearly a third of the system. Experts say that fixing a system this large is a tall order, partly because the current system is so old. “If you own a car for 30 years, it’s going to be increasingly difficult as the car gets older to find the replacement parts you need to keep it in operating condition. The same is true of any kind of technology serving any kind of industry,” said Henry Harteveldt, president of Atmosphere Research Group and a travel industry analyst. “There are many parts of airline and aviation technology that are no longer fit due to their age.” And Friday afternoon, the painstaking efforts to keep that antiquated air traffic control system functioning caught up with the Federal Aviation Administration and the more than one million on-board and would-be passengers. The problems arose when a contractor was working to replace some of the copper wire with fiber optics. “That new equipment, new technology just was overwhelming the older system,” said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “The patchwork doesn’t work.” The part of the air traffic control system that monitors and communicates with planes at their cruising altitude was no longer reliable enough to keep those planes in the air or allow new planes to take off. So, the FAA ordered a rare systemwide “ground stop,” leading to 9,200 canceled flights, according to tracking service FlightAware. And even though the ground stop was lifted just after 8 p.m. ET on Friday, many flights could not be started at that point due to staffing issues or the lack of planes being in the right city. So another 6,200 were canceled on Saturday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem is coming up with a modern system while keeping the current antiquated system up and running. “I don’t want to lie to anybody,” he said Friday night at the same press conference. “What we’re doing is hard, and it hasn’t happened in the past because it is hard. But I’ll tell you, by doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system. “We use 1980s technology, 1990s software, to use 1970s radar that we don’t make parts for anymore,” he said. Earlier problems from old systems Friday’s ground stop wasn’t the first time the aging infrastructure has disrupted travel. Communication issues with the air traffic control systems directing flights around heavily trafficked Newark Liberty Airport in May 2025 caused the FAA to limit the number of flights and resulted in air traffic controllers becoming so stressed from not being able to communicate with planes that some workers took trauma leave, causing a staffing shortage to worsen. In a similar situation to Friday’s grounding of flights, in January 2023, the system used to notify pilots of their route’s conditions went down, grounding all flights. Airlines also have old technology It’s not just the FAA that copes with older technology. Even the actual airlines use outdated tools. In July 2024, an automatic update from cybersecurity software provider CrowdStrike caused massive problems on Windows computers, which impacted companies all around the world and required a restart of computers. But no company had a harder time restarting normal operations than Delta Air Lines, which had greater problems bringing its crew-tracking software back online, leaving it unable to staff airplanes. A massive problem at Southwest Airlines during the 2022 year-end holidays resulted in 16,700 canceled flights, millions of passengers scrambling to complete their holiday travel and costing the airline at least $1 billion. Much of it was due to problems with its own antiquated crew scheduling system, which required phone calls between the airline and crew members rather than online check-ins — a system that would make it impossible for the airline to find the crews it needed to staff flights. Harteveldt, the travel analyst, said Southwest has spent at least $1.3 billion  since then upgrading its technology, hardware, software and communications networks. “We have a much better understanding of our crew network and are able to work in real time to adjust to unexpected circumstances,” Southwest said Saturday in response to a question about its upgrades. Hesitance to pay for new tech Airlines can be reluctant to fund back-office technology upgrades when they can instead spend on ways to attract more passengers, such as better Wi-Fi, newer planes and upgraded airport lounges, said Harteveldt. “They are risk-averse, and so they want to be sure that whatever technology they do end up investing in is a technology that will be useful long term to the airline,” he said. “That’s another reason why airlines tend to be technology laggards. They also just don’t have the profit margins, even in the best of years, to allocate large sums to technology upgrades.” The FAA’s problems are strictly political: it needs Congress to approve funding. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control upgrades, and before Friday, Duffy had asked for another $30 billion. On Friday night, he said the agency now needs $50 billion. It’s possible the mess at the nation’s airports on Friday night will help win support for that greater Congressional spending. But the problems have existed for years. And even if the FAA has unlimited funds, it’s clear from the problems created by Friday’s attempted upgrade of existing systems that it won’t be repeated in the future. “Is this exact thing going to happen again? I don’t know,” Duffy said. “I think there’s no better time than the present to actually give us the money and let us finish.”

cnn.com.title: Europe scrambles to respond to wave of bomb threats disrupting transport, media and schools
cnn.com.text: An unprecedented wave of bomb threats across Europe has left the bloc struggling to respond, as it remains unclear who is behind the incidents. The threats, which are mainly understood to have been sent via emails and have so far all proven false, have impacted multiple media broadcasters, more than 50 flights, thousands of schools and at least one cruise ship across the continent, posing an increasingly urgent security challenge for European authorities. Analysts say the hoaxes have exposed the vulnerability of Europe’s public infrastructure to anonymous and hard-to-trace messages and highlight the bloc’s need for a more coordinated response. The bomb threats targeting European flights were taken seriously by authorities and elicited strong action, which varied between countries. While some authorities diverted flights to other airports, others – such as Hungary and France – scrambled fighter jets to escort the affected passenger planes. Some are calling for European countries to replace fragmented, nation-by-nation reactions with a bloc-wide security framework. The chief executive of budget Hungarian airline Wizz Air, József Váradi, spoke Thursday of the need for more harmonized security procedures and alluded to the possible creation of a central body to manage such hoaxes. He revealed that he had recently held a meeting with European Commission officials to push for a coordinated response. “But this is a very hot potato because of the sovereign nation state concept, and no country wants to concede on this matter, ” Váradi said in a post-earnings call Thursday. ‘Scrambled response’ A threat targeting an airline operating across several countries could involve several law enforcement agencies, meaning that greater information-sharing between countries could prove key to identifying patterns and determining the origin and validity of the threat. Grégoire Roos, director of the Europe, Russia and Eurasia programs at the London-based Chatham House think tank, said that while the initial security responses had been strong, coordination between European countries remains insufficient. At present, each country is responding with “its own toolbox and standards,” due to the threats being a relatively new phenomenon, he told CNN. A first step for improvement, he believes, would be to establish a Europe-wide threat assessment standard. “For instance, emergency measures should depend on corroborating intelligence and the circumstances of each incident at continental level.” He also believes that whoever is behind the attacks is exploiting differences in national procedures. “Europol, national police, in some cases even regional police forces, aviation authorities, all need to compare technical evidence. “So, you have in a way a scrambled response and within that scrambled response you have sub-levels. So, it increases the response time, and it therefore gives more space for anxiety to grow.” The threats also expose that while it is cheap to launch such hoaxes, it is vastly more expensive to counter them. A single email can force a mass security deployment, divert flights or prompt the evacuation of public buildings. Such methods weigh heavily on public resources, cause disruption to daily life and sow public unease. School evacuations One response has been to try to carry on as normal. When thousands of schools in Italy received a threat this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s overarching message to concerned parents was to remain calm and keep disruption to a minimum. Bomb threats were sent via email to around 6,300 Italian schools on Wednesday and around 3,778 on Thursday. While hundreds of schools were evacuated, many also chose to remain open. Meloni proposed new evacuation protocols in the wake of the threats, stipulating that schools should not be evacuated based solely on a mass email and without concrete evidence. Schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland also received threatening emails Wednesday. Police warned these were likely hoaxes and education facilities were not evacuated. Meanwhile some UK airports made the decision to remain open despite receiving threats. “As far as the UK is concerned, we’ve seen the airports of Heathrow and Birmingham that managed to continue operating after they received threats, because those were assessed as not credible. So, I think this is something others across Europe could do, rather than saying ‘OK there’s a minor alert, we’ll close everything,’” Roos said. He added, “It matters more than you think, because the moment you evacuate it increases the level of anxiety.” The digital nature of the alerts – the vast majority of them were sent via email – makes it difficult for investigators to track down their origin. While some of them were signed off by certain entities, such as the “Male State,” a Russian ultra-nationalist group, authorities suspect these could be false attributions. Cybersecurity firms Proofpoint and Abnormal Security found a large portion of the threats were sent from legitimate webmail accounts that had been hijacked. Such practices make it difficult for law enforcement to track down those responsible and can keep authorities stuck in a reactive posture. Russia suspicions There are strong suspicions that the incidents could be part of a wider campaign of so-called hybrid warfare, in which hostile actors seek to undermine public confidence and destabilize countries without resorting to conventional military force. European officials have increasingly warned about the threat posed by such tactics, with Russia frequently accused of using cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to undermine Western countries. Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in such activities. But French President Emmanuel Macron cautioned against jumping to conclusions over the wave of bomb threats, saying Thursday that there was not yet the evidence to attribute them to foreign powers. “As I speak, we do not have sufficient elements to be able to make an attribution,” Macron told reporters during a meeting of European leaders in Dublin. Roos warned against automatically pointing the finger at Moscow without concrete evidence, saying that this could embolden potential other actors. “We run the risk of empowering, for lack of a better word, many other perpetrators, both state- and non-state actors, if each time there is a threat we immediately attribute it to Moscow without even looking into it,” he said. It also remains unclear whether the threats spanning schools, airlines, broadcasters and other institutions are connected, or whether they originate from a single individual, group or state-backed operation. For now, the challenge is striking the balance between taking every potential threat seriously and ensuring that the anonymous emails do not repeatedly bring essential services to a standstill. As the incidents continue to go beyond national borders, pressure is likely to grow on European governments to establish a more coordinated approach — one that can distinguish credible security threats from attempts to exploit the very precautions designed to protect the public.

bbc.com.title: Wife of assassinated ex-Haitian leader registers for presidential election
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation.
Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021.
Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence.
Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity.
Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday.
Last week she said on X: "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently."
A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy.
Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021, allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries.
Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds during the attack and was flown to a hospital in Florida.
She was charged in connection with the assassination in 2024, but the indictment was overturned last year.
The assassination shook the Caribbean nation to its core, with many Haitians shocked that the 53-year-old was killed with such apparent ease.
Thirty suspects have been indicted over the killing so far and in September 18 people were flown from Haiti to Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination.
Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Moise.
At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti.

bbc.com.title: Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
bbc.com.text:
Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
A teenage girl and her cat have been reunited four days after a building in the New York borough of Brooklyn collapsed.
Zariah Coleman, 13, made an emotional plea when her pet went missing after she and her family were forced to relocate when the side of their building was stripped off in the unexpected collapse.
City officials later found her cat, Isaac, in the debris of the their home and shared the reunion on Sunday afternoon.
Eight people died and 18 others were injured when the three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood last Wednesday.

bbc.com.title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.
Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.
Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.
At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.
The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.
He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.
At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.
At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.
In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena.
Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.
His murder sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.
In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was granted house arrest in 2022 but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer. He died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.
In the 1980s, Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.
From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.
In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.
Félix Gallardo's life has been portrayed in a number of television programmes including the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. The show depicted his rise to power as well as his relationship with Guzmán.

bbc.com.title: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.
The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.
In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.
"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.
"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."
She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.
Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family.
"All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement.
"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."

bbc.com.title: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
bbc.com.text:
- Published
