Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.
Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
The Reuters news agency reported a Southern Armed Forces statement which said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".
It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

bbc.com.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
But while Alice Huang is said to have stepped down from her role as Megaspeed director near the end of 2023, there were suspicions that she was still heavily involved in the firm's operations, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS
C4ADS said that Huang was still "practically in control" of Megaspeed even after she had handed over the reins of the firm.
Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.
Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.
Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.
"That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme.
Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded.
The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated to lead Nvidia is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing.
The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside the company.
On Friday, Bessent had blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia

bbc.com.title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
bbc.com.text:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.
More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.
Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.
"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."
In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.
That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.
And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.
But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.
The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.
Restless tycoons
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule". They had money, which back then meant power.
This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.
But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.
Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.
"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.
Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn).
But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.
Autocracy, oligarchy or democracy?
Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.
"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."
And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.
"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.
And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.
There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."
If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.
In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.
Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.
Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.
And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.
This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.
Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.
Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".
He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says.
Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name.
Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians.
But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says.
A bombshell interview
An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man.
Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him.
In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty.
But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world.
Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says.
The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin.
Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country.
No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen.
Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge.
Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia to… [an] absence of the future".
But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems.
Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man."
Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen."
Russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them?

bbc.com.title: Steering failure preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The tanker that struck a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday had a steering failure, officials said, citing preliminary findings into the collision.
It remains unclear what caused the "steering casualty" on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a media briefing on Sunday.
The collision left 32 people from the stricken American Heritage riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for.
The NTSB said there are many different things that could be classified as a steering casualty, and they are "looking at all of them".
The tanker was upbound on the Mississippi River as it moved toward the east bank of the river just before the collision, said the NTSB, based on findings from the vessel's voyage data recorder.
Minutes before the crash, investigators said audio consistent with the ship's warning system was broadcast, along with commands to deploy the vessel's anchors and emergency ship handling orders.
"We are aware that there was an issue with the steering on board and causing the rudder to remain at a starboard position, causing the heading of the vessel to veer towards the east bank," investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said during the news conference.
The exact issue with the steering has yet to be determined, he added.
A preliminary report from the NTSB is expected in 30 days.
Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll said after the incident.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.
Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side.
Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.
The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

bbc.com.title: Canada bars Russia from Junior World Championships
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Russia's hopes of reintegration into international sport suffered a setback when it was barred from the upcoming Junior Ice Hockey World Championships.
Canada said it would deny entry to Russian athletes as a result of the war in Ukraine.
"Due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian government, the Russian Under-20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship," the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement.
It said that "after carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer."
The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable and unlawful" and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
"The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons," it said in a statement.
"The exclusion of the Russian national team violates fundamental legal principles, Olympism, the principle of non-discrimination, equality among athletes and the integrity of international tournaments."
Russia had been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, but last month the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned the ban.
It said that the IIHF's arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence" and ordered it to allow Russia to participate in its events.
The move was welcomed by Russia but condemned by Ukraine and along with some sponsors of the Junior World Championships.
Six European ice hockey federations said they would refuse to play Russia if they were allowed to take part, appearing to leave the tournament in limbo.
On Wednesday the Canadian government said it would deny visas to any Russian athletes, effectively barring them from participating.
It is the latest example of a wider backlash against efforts to allow Russia to return to international sport.
This week Norway, Finland and Estonia said they would block visas for Russian and Belarusian athletes.
Norway is preparing to host skiing's Cross-country World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the Figure Skating World Championships in March.
The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.
In March several athletes from Russia and Belarus were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.
In July the IOC provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, saying a ban introduced in 2023 was "no longer applicable".
However, sports federations can enforce their own eligibility criteria.
While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.
Last month it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the invasion of Ukraine.

bbc.com.title: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."
Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.
Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.
A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.
At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.
International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.
In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
At a noisy sports centre, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.
He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.
He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.
And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.
Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.
He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.
At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"These people have so much to offer," he said.
"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

bbc.com.title: Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the licence fee and use the state budget to fund public media.
Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.
The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.
Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.
Czech households currently pay 205 crowns ($9.44; £7.06) a month for public TV and radio.
Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.
"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.
"If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."
Prime Minister Andrej Babis has insisted the government does not want to control public media.
"The funding system is changing, no one wants to control public media, no one wants to dictate to them what they should say and do, no one wants to nationalise them," Babis told the Czech News Agency.
"We are doing this because the system is already outdated and most of Europe is going the same way today and others are joining in," he added.
Some European countries, including France and Norway, have moved away from the public licence fee model in the last few years.
France removed it in 2022 and its public media, which also carries advertising, is now funded by a portion of the income from VAT.
Norway abolished its license fee in 2020 and moved its public broadcaster's funding into the national budget.
Reuters said the proposal would amount to a 15% cut in funding for the public broadcasters Czech TV and Czech Radio.
Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Vecernicek, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.
Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power.
Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media.
"Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June.

bbc.com.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.
The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade service developed by Elon Musk's Starlink and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.
Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.
On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".
"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.
"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try to carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

bbc.com.title: Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
bbc.com.text:
Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America.
Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory".
On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire.
There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love."
The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope.
He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.

bbc.com.title: How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
bbc.com.text:
- Published
An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.
Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday.
US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers.
Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe.
Here's what we know.
What caused the stoppage?
On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network.
As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.
According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.
As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.
This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted.
As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."
Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag.
In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage.
He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day.
In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation.
"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said.
Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel.
"You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said
"You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added.
A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel".
He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
How many flights were affected?
The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.
The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.
The FAA opened skies again at 20:15 EST.
What about international flights?
All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended.
There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.
Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning.
A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport.
Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned.
Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada.
When will normal service resume?
Duffy said on Saturday: "We are back at full operations."
But, as he predicted on Friday, it is taking time to unwind what happened.
FlightAware said more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and more than 7,000 delayed in the US on Saturday.
Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations but they both cancelled 20% of their flights on Saturday. American Airlines cancelled 520 journeys.
Meanwhile, JetBlue cancelled 40% of its scheduled journeys.
By Sunday morning, the situation had improved, but the impacts of the stoppage were still being felt with more than 2,400 flights delayed and 1,400 cancelled.
What are your rights?
In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.
As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.
But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws.
Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly.
It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.
In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers.
However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights.
Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.
This includes:
- a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers)
- a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)
- free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next day
- transport to and from that accommodation
If your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.
The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.
When was the last ground stop?
It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.
"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.
Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.
"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.
The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published and flights were grounded until that system was restored.

bbc.com.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.
The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.
Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.
"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."
When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.
He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.
"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.
The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.
The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".
Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.
The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.
Can smart glasses exam cheating be stopped?
Asia Specific
A series of cases involving exam cheating with AI glasses in South Korea has universities and schools scrambling to rein in the use of the technology.
Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.
Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.
"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.
It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.
Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.
Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.
Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

aljazeera.com.title: US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline
aljazeera.com.text:
A tense race to replace outgoing United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is heading into its final few weeks in advance of a deadline that has never been breached, as global powers spar over candidates in an opaque election process.
With eight candidates, secret polls and geopolitical rivalries at play, the choice of the UN’s next chief is still up in the air, even as Guterres must leave office on December 31.
Competing interests from the Americas to the Middle East have complicated the process, raising fears that, for the first time in history, the new year could begin without a leader at the helm of the world’s central diplomatic organisation. The late inclusion of two candidates — Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh and Turkish nominee Feridun Sinirlioglu — has further split the race wide open, with no name so far succeeding in overcoming opposition from all five permanent members of the UN Security Council (UNSC), who hold vetoes.
The protracted contest is part of a “struggle over who will exercise political influence within the UN at a time when multilateralism is under considerable pressure and attack”, Georgina Holmes, senior lecturer in politics and international studies at the Open University, United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.
“P5 member states are not as politically aligned as they have been in previous eras, arguably even during the Cold War,” said Holmes, referring to the permanent members of the UNSC.
‘Most difficult job in the world’
The UN secretary-general has often been compared with a “secular pope” – a figure expected to unite countries and spearhead global diplomacy.
But the position is more than that of a figurehead. The secretary-general is also the UN’s top administrative official, responsible for tapping senior officials and supervising the UN Secretariat’s tens of thousands of staff.
“The secretary-general must be a skilled politician to navigate the geopolitics; a skilled diplomat and mediator to help settle disputes; a charismatic person in the public eye; and a solid and skilled administrator,” Jan Klabbers, professor of international law at the University of Cambridge, told Al Jazeera. “It has been called ‘the most difficult job in the world’ for a reason.”
This year’s race comes as the UN, under Guterres, is under heavy strain, having been sidelined from conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. It has faced blistering criticism from United States President Donald Trump and is suffering a financial crisis that has forced it to let go of thousands of staff.
It also comes as wider geopolitical rivalries extend to the pool of candidates to lead the organisation, who are being scrutinised over their nationalities and policy commitments.
Who is in the running?
Eight individuals who have been appointed by UN member states are currently in the running to replace Guterres. Most of them are from Latin America or the Caribbean, which is in line with representation according to informal UN protocol. Five of the eight are women, amid a push for the UN to select its first female secretary-general.
A leading contender, according to a series of anonymous straw polls the UNSC carries out to gauge support, is Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan.
In the last poll on November 5, which does not show which UNSC members voted which way, Grynspan received 12 “encourage” votes and three “discourage” votes, according to PassBlue, a nonprofit that reports on UN affairs.
Grynspan, who heads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), has been described as a “continuity candidate”, but there are concerns as to whether she would bring enough reform to an organisation facing huge political and financial pressures.
Richard Gowan, programme director of global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Grynspan had “solidified her position as the frontrunner”, but still appears to face opposition from the US and Russia, which could veto her bid.
While she has avoided directly confronting any veto-wielding nation, some of her reports as UNCTAD head have voiced concerns over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, positions at odds with Washington’s more full-throated support for Israel. Grynspan has previously also disagreed with Russian justifications for suspending a deal to allow the transport of grain through the Black Sea.
At the same time, she — like other candidates — is believed to be lobbying with key member states to win their support. In April, she met Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov over her candidature.
“Grynspan’s team argue that they can still nudge Washington and Moscow to accept her, and US officials do seem to be leaving open the possibility of working with her in the end,” said Gowan.
To be elected, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour in the 15-member UNSC, while avoiding any vetoes from its five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGA) then ultimately has to sign off.
Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society campaign “advocating for a fair, open, inclusive way to select the next secretary-general”, stressed that opposition from P5 members in a straw poll does not necessarily equate to an eventual veto.
“It has been used in the past as a basis to extract a concession from a candidate, very often in the form of a backroom deal to get a P5 national appointed to a key role in the future UN boss’s cabinet,” he told Al Jazeera.
The Argentinian head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, is also in the running. He finished second in the latest straw poll, with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes. However, his reputation for being closely aligned with Washington is expected to hurt him with some P5 members, especially China and Russia, though he has also had warm words for Beijing and Moscow in recent weeks.
The other candidates from Latin America or the Caribbean are Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Antigua and Barbuda diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.
Rodrigues Birkett, whose description of Israel’s actions in Gaza as “genocide” has drawn scrutiny in the US, received five “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll. Espinosa and A-Baki received 10 and 14 “discourage” votes, respectively, making their candidacies unlikely.
The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh and Turkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioglu, nominated by their countries in recent weeks, have also shaken up the race but face significant opposition.
Nusseibeh is reportedly favoured by the US and Russia, but her candidacy has received pushback over her country’s alleged arming of paramilitary forces accused of atrocities in Sudan. The United Arab Emirates has denied the allegation. Nusseibeh received six “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll.
“Nusseibeh’s main challenge is to win over China, which has so far seemed sceptical about her candidacy,” said Gowan. “If she can get Beijing’s support, she could break through.”
Sinirlioglu’s candidature, which UNSC member Greece is expected to oppose, received eight “discourage” votes.
Ugandan politician Olara Otunnu, the only remaining African candidate, received nine “discourage” votes.
Far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, though not an official candidate, has also been floated by the US as an outside choice, The Wall Street Journal has reported.
UN in ‘near-constant crisis’
Several analysts told Al Jazeera that Grynspan appears to be in the best position, though the influence of P5 countries could change the race.
Earlier this month, the US and Russia put their weight behind the UAE’s Nusseibeh, with France and the UK offering “little resistance”, according to diplomats cited by media platform Devex.
China, for its part, has signalled a preference for a Latin American candidate, reports The New York Times, although Beijing has not publicly endorsed anyone.
Ellen Ravndal, associate professor in political science at the University of Stavanger, Norway, told Al Jazeera the drawn-out selection process and struggle to reach consensus reflect an era of “more geopolitical tensions” and a UN that is in “near-constant crisis mode”.
Adam Day, head of the Geneva office of the United Nations University Centre for Policy Research, pointed out that while the leadership contest has been lengthier and more contested than in the previous cycles in which former Secretaries-General Guterres in 2016 and Ban Ki-moon in 2006 were elected, some earlier races stretched into December.
“In the broader scope of secretary-general races, this one is still within the range of what has been normal,” Day told Al Jazeera. “But the longer it takes, the less time the incoming secretary-general has to prepare a transition.”
If no successor to Guterres is selected by the end of the year, the UN Charter does not specify an automatic interim successor. Any gap in the post would therefore require the UNSC and other UN bodies to agree on how to manage organisational leadership and operations.
“There is widespread concern that the United States and possibly other influential states are running down the clock, potentially to increase pressure to settle for a less popular candidate or to leave the UN leaderless and weakened for a period,” said Donaldson.

aljazeera.com.title: Widow of Haiti’s slain leader Moise to contest presidential vote
aljazeera.com.text:
The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 assassination was a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.
Martine Moise’s name appeared on the website of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) as a candidate on Sunday.
A first-round vote is set for July next year.
Haiti last held a presidential election in 2016. Successive leaders have repeatedly delayed elections, citing insecurity risks, amid the expanding influence of powerful and heavily armed gangs.
“Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently,” Moise, who has not publicly commented on the registration, said on X last week.
In the post, she also blamed “the opposition” for bringing the country “to its knees”. “They do not want the country to develop; they do not want the people to live well,” she said.
Three female candidates
Martine Moise is one of three women among 33 registered presidential candidates. Among other prominent candidates are Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, both former presidents, former Prime Minister Claude Joseph and former Foreign Minister Dominique Dupuy.
Several candidates, including Martelly and Privert, have been sanctioned internationally over accusations, which they both deny, of supporting armed gangs.
Martine Moise has been a key witness in the Miami court case prosecuting dozens of suspects involved in the murder of her husband, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death in July 2021.
He was shot in his bedroom by Colombian mercenaries impersonating agents of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration. Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds and was flown to a hospital in Florida.
A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and surrounding regions.
Tens of thousands killed
About 1.5 million people have been displaced and more than 22,000 have been killed, many by security personnel. Several international forces have been deployed to Haiti to help police fight the gangs; the most recent deployment, last month, involved soldiers from El Salvador.
Last week, Haitian security forces regained control of the country’s main stadium, which had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.
The operation was part of a deployment of about 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, who announced that the troops would set up an operational base in the stadium to push further into territory still controlled by the gangs.

aljazeera.com.title: Iraqi armed group denies involvement in oil smuggling, calls probe a ‘lie’
aljazeera.com.text:
The Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah group has denied its involvement in an oil smuggling operation in Iraq’s Jurf al-Nasr area after Iraqi authorities launched an anticorruption crackdown.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, said in a statement on Sunday that the Iraqi prime minister’s office was “fabricating lies” and that the group was being subjected to “the largest blackmail operation” to force its disarmament.
The statement was issued a day after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi sacked nine senior officials following an investigation into the allegations.
The Iraqi government said an investigation committee, chaired by al-Zaidi, confirmed oil smuggling based on “intelligence documents” containing satellite images showing operations being carried out in the armed faction’s stronghold.
The committee ordered those implicated, whom it did not identify, to be referred to the judiciary and dismissed nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.
Responding to the committee’s findings, Kataib Hezbollah said the investigation “found no violations whatsoever of the oil pipelines” and that this “definitively proves that the smuggling allegations are false”.
The group said its members accompanied the committee’s visit to the Jurf al-Nasr area on Friday.
Baghdad has been under increasing pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned groups and curb Tehran’s influence in Iraq, an ally of both the US and Iran.
Al-Zaidi has previously promised to ensure that non-state armed groups would hand over their weapons to the state.
However, Kataib Hezbollah has pledged to retain its weapons arsenal and accused al-Zaidi of caving to pressure from the US, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Iran-aligned groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have previously targeted US forces in Iraq and attacked Gulf states following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.
Washington accuses Tehran of using Iraq’s economy to evade sanctions and has previously sanctioned Iraqi individuals for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.

aljazeera.com.title: Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, says Alice Huang left in 2025
aljazeera.com.text:
Megaspeed has confirmed that Alice Huang, the tech executive whose reported relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of international spying claims, left the company last year.
The Singapore-based data centre company said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang left her executive role on August 30, 2025, and has held no position with the firm since.
“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters,” the statement said.
Megaspeed also pushed back on media reports it said contained claims about its operations that “are not supported by verifiable evidence”.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said.
Megaspeed, a major buyer of graphics processing units (GPUs) made by the California-based Nvidia, used to train and run frontier AI models, is facing scrutiny over its compliance with United States export controls intended to keep high-end chips out of China.
While data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand can import high-end Nvidia chips legally, US authorities have long suspected the region is a hotbed of illicit smuggling on behalf of Chinese AI developers.
Megaspeed CEO and chairman Tan Yong Pong said on Thursday that the company had retained a top US law firm to lead a “comprehensive census” of its GPUs and verify its export control compliance practices.
Unnamed US officials have accused Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security in an espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia CEO, president and board member on Thursday amid a board investigation.
Beijing has denied the allegations, describing them as “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims.
Singaporean authorities are investigating Megaspeed on suspicion of making false declarations in relation to its purchases of servers. They said last week they had previously confiscated Alice Huang’s passport for eight months as part of their inquiries.
Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday that it barred Huang from re-entering the country after determining that she had provided inaccurate information to investigators to downplay her role at Megaspeed.
Police investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals are ongoing, the ministry said in a statement.

aljazeera.com.title: Indonesian president apologises to Singapore, Malaysia for wildfire haze
aljazeera.com.text:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has apologised to Singapore and Malaysia for the transboundary haze due to months-long wildfires.
Prabowo conveyed the apology during a session at the ASEAN summit that kicked off on Sunday in the Philippine capital, Manila, according to a statement from the Indonesian presidential office.
“I would like to apologise to my neighbouring countries Malaysia and Singapore when we had a very big forest fire, which took nearly four months for us to control. The haze travelled to Malaysia and to Singapore. It is not not our fault but once again we apologise but we have done our best,” he said.
Prabowo also said his government had and would continue to take firm action on companies involved in forest fires while also preparing to establish a new body to strengthen wildfire prevention.
Indonesia has a “zero-tolerance policy” for any company contributing to the blazes, the statement quoted him as saying.
“We’ve revoked 17 concessions [permits] from companies. [Meanwhile] 26 companies are currently under investigation and 11 others have been charged. Another 23 companies are on the list to be charged,” he said.
“In total, 104 companies are currently under investigation by our police.”
He also said Indonesia had deployed 71,000 forest firefighters, and 16 people died while battling the blazes.
Philippine Foreign Minister Theresa Lazaro told a news briefing later on Sunday that Jakarta was “very frank and candid in expressing the efforts they have been exerting in addressing the forest fires in Indonesia” during the plenary session.
Indonesia has been battling its most intense wildfires in 11 years, with large swaths of land scorched, mainly on the islands of Sumatra, Borneo and Papua.
Haze from the fires blanketed some of its nearest neighbours, primarily Singapore and Malaysia, over the past few months.
Malaysia and Singapore have refrained from criticising Indonesia, instead offering assistance to fight the fires.
Previously, an Indonesian official faced criticism after claiming the country’s forests supply oxygen to Malaysia and Singapore despite recurring haze from wildfires.
“We do not just send smoke, but when there is no smoke, we send oxygen,” Indonesian Government Communications Agency chief Syahganda Nainggolan said in October.
ASEAN agreement
On paper, Southeast Asian countries are committed to working together to prevent cross-border air pollution under the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The legally binding treaty commits the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to tackle haze, a recurring issue for decades, through “concerted national efforts and intensified regional and international co-operation”.
However, the agreement does not contain provisions for enforcement by a judicial body such as the International Court of Justice. Disagreements over interpretation and application can only be settled through negotiation.
Implementation of the treaty has also moved at a snail’s pace. The treaty’s coordinating office in Jakarta only opened this April, nearly a quarter-century after it was envisioned.
Prabowo’s remarks came as the problem of transboundary haze has begun to disappear.
On Thursday, the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) issued a “no transboundary smoke haze” notice for southern parts of Southeast Asia, the Jakarta Post reported. The relief has been linked to recent downpours and fewer fire hotspots in Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces.

Pope Leo flies to mass in the Papacoptero
