npr.org.title: New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
npr.org.text:
New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
It's a hazy August morning, and Judyn Martinez is dropping her daughter off at Kids Campus, a sought-after childcare center in Santa Fe that is now free for any eligible family in New Mexico.
"It's an amazing school so far. She loves it. I love it," Martinez said. "Everyone's nice. She's learning, growing already."
A year ago this month, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every family, regardless of income. To qualify, families must be residents of New Mexico and adults in the house must be working, looking for work, in school or unable to work.
Many parents, including Martinez, told NPR that it's been life-changing.
"I'm really grateful for universal childcare because I wouldn't have been able to send her," Martinez said.
There's just one drawback for families: Right now, the state doesn't have the capacity to meet the demand, which has left some families waiting without childcare. Martinez said it took her about a year and half to get off the waitlist for Kids Campus — a waitlist that, today, has nearly 700 children on it.
When she first spoke with NPR in September, Lilia Doyle said her 2-year-old son was on six different waitlists.
"I'm 97th on a multi-hundred person waitlist. I'm 75th on something. And some, I'm not even getting calls back," Doyle said.
Doyle, a children's librarian with a background in early childhood education, lives in Santa Fe. She acknowledged that she's selective when it comes to childcare. Still, she said, it should be easier.
"I have great belief in this program, but as it currently stands, I think the rollout needs a lot, a lot of help."
According to the state, New Mexico has about 67,000 children 5 and under, and about 50% of them are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other free public programs, like New Mexico PreK and Head Start.
But many children aren't enrolled in any public, free childcare program, and it's hard to know exactly how many are in Doyle's position, unable to access universal childcare because of limited capacity. New Mexico officials acknowledged to NPR that the program needs to expand.
In order to work for every family, the program will have to overcome both a shortage of childcare workers and childcare slots — two challenges that are also playing out at the national level.
Because of that, across the country, policymakers and childcare advocates are keeping a close eye on this Southwestern experiment.
Cynthia Osborne, who leads Vanderbilt University's Prenatal-to-3 Policy Impact Center, said New Mexico is "going to provide lessons that the rest of the states are going to have to pay attention to."
"If New Mexico can show us how to build the infrastructure, I think other states will say that's an investment that we should make."
But the challenges to building that infrastructure – and keeping costs under control – are very real.
The program has built-in safeguards in case economic downturns make it harder to pay for – and one of those safeguards was recently triggered: The annual Consumer Price Index rose above 3%, which means wealthier families – who make more than $198,000 for a household of four – will soon have to start making a copayment. According to the state's Early Childhood Education and Care Department, ECECD, that copay won't exceed $148.50 a month. The department says this change will affect about 10% of enrolled families, and will remain in effect through the fiscal year.
How it happened in New Mexico
Like many states, New Mexico previously offered childcare subsidies to low-income families, and free childcare to the lowest-income families. For a while, the state was raising the income limits for those programs.
Families, providers and grassroots organizers had also been campaigning to do away with those limits entirely. One of the big sticking points was how to pay for it, and the answer came in 2022, when New Mexicans voted to dedicate a portion of the state's Land Grant Permanent Fund to early childhood education. Much of that fund consists of taxes and royalties on the state's vast oil and gas production, and it's large enough to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to support childcare every year.
Then, in September 2025, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a plan for free, universal childcare and prekindergarten, which would begin Nov. 1 of that year. After it launched, the program was approved by the Democrat-majority state legislature and was officially written into law in March 2026.
Any licensed or registered childcare provider in New Mexico can participate in the program. The state offers higher reimbursements for centers that pay workers higher wages and operate a minimum of 10 hours, five days a week.
"I think childcare is a gamechanger for every single thing that a state ought to deliver for its families," Lujan Grisham told NPR.
The governor said this year is going "stunningly well."
"I can't go anywhere in New Mexico… where I don't have a parent tell me that this is life-changing and transformative," she said.
But she knows more capacity is needed.
"We need to keep growing," Lujan Grisham said. "It is not a stagnant set of opportunities."
In 2025, ECECD set a goal to create 12,000 new childcare spots in the first few years of the program, but did not share a specific deadline with NPR. According to the department, they are more than halfway there.
A nationwide childcare shortage
It was no surprise that accessibility would be an issue for a program like this.
Nearly half of all U.S. children, ages 5 and under, live in a licensed childcare desert, where demand for care outpaces availability, according to the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank.
Olga Grays, a childcare provider for more than 20 years, said she fields messages every day from desperate parents who she isn't able to give slots to. That's one reason she's part of a group chat that includes over 40 childcare providers in her area.
"Every time somebody calls me, you know, I put their name and the age of their kids in that group. And I'm like, 'Does anybody have openings?' You know, but the sad thing is that not a lot of people have openings, especially for infants."
Grays, a single mother of five, operates out of her home in Las Cruces, in the southern part of the state.
At Mrs. Olga's Daycare, the living room has been transformed into a classroom, with cushioned, fall-safe floors. The outdoor space is part children's playground and part garden oasis.
"[The children] can play with water, with dirt, grass. They ground themselves. It makes a world of a difference," Grays said.
She wishes she didn't have to turn any children away.
"I think that's one of our biggest issues right now, is making sure that we have enough spots available for everybody coming in," Grays said. "And I think that's one of the flaws that perhaps other states can learn from."
According to the Center for American Progress, rural areas especially struggle with childcare deserts — and New Mexico is very rural.
"It's not a lack of funding, it's a lack of providers," the state's speaker of the house, Javier Martinez, told NPR. He's a Democrat and an advocate for universal childcare. "We have communities that are miles from any type of population center. Hundreds of miles sometimes. And so there are communities where that market isn't quite there to support a business."
The tension around providing free childcare to wealthier families
The program's current operating budget is almost $600 million.
But there's concern among some state lawmakers that it's projected to be about $50 million over budget this year.
"By calling it universal, all we've done is add the wealthier folks," said state Sen. Steve Lanier, a Republican representing the northwest corner of New Mexico.
Lanier sued to stop the governor's universal childcare initiative — a lawsuit that was ultimately unsuccessful.
He told NPR that the steep price tag for this program is why he only supports childcare assistance for some.
"My daughter's a school teacher. She has two young boys. She gets free childcare. So, from a personal view, I see where it is needed. I mean, that helps her and her family immensely," Lanier said. "But somebody that's making $450,000, $600,000, do they really need that assistance?"
Catron Allred, who oversees the early childhood center at Santa Fe Community College, doesn't see it that way.
"To me, I think it's a mentality of early childhood as a public good," she explained. "Nobody questions a wealthy family sending their kids to public school and it should be the same for early childhood."
It's not a one-size-fits-all model
While New Mexico is the only state with free, universal childcare right now, other states and cities have made progress in that direction, including Oregon, Connecticut, Washington, D.C., New York City and Vermont, which has tapped into payroll taxes for funding.
In New York City, which already has free prekindergarten for 3- and 4-year-olds, Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently rolled out free daycare for thousands of the city's 2-year-olds.
As in New Mexico, "Both the biggest challenge and opportunity in New York City is our scale," explained Emmy Liss, executive director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education.
"We know that every family's childcare needs are different. We know that our diverse landscape of childcare providers offer a really wide mix of services that families value," Liss added. "But to build a system that incorporates all of those different providers and meets the needs of all of our families is a complex challenge."
Liss said the goal is to have free pre-k for every 2-year-old by the end of the mayor's first term. But instead of expanding access to everyone all at once, as New Mexico has done, she said the city is growing capacity "in parallel" with access by creating more slots and matching them with families.
"We are working to build the infrastructure, the workforce, the physical capacity and the support to providers to ensure that we can continue to scale access to care here," Liss told NPR.
She said her office has been in conversation with leaders in New Mexico, and has had the chance to learn from them. But ultimately, she said, "Our realities are different."
"I think we're making slightly different choices in how we are implementing expanded access to care, which is good. I think we should be making different choices, responsive to the needs we hear from New Yorkers."
Childcare can make or break a parent's work life
Veronica Ramirez lives in Ohkay Owingeh, a federally recognized tribe and pueblo in northern New Mexico. She said she learned about universal childcare when it was in the news last year and decided to enroll her 2-year-old daughter.
"For my daughter, I think it's really opened doors for her," Ramirez told NPR.
"Just being able to be around other little human beings that are her age...I've seen her go up to other little kids in public and say hi or just start playing with them. And I'm like, 'Oh, well, she's social now. She's not clinging to mom only.' "
For Ramirez, having consistent childcare has enabled her to do more nonprofit work, including as an outreach coordinator at a birth center that primarily serves indigenous clients in nearby Española. It helps that her 7-year-old son is in school for the same hours as her daughter is in daycare.
"Now I'm able to work more and make more money and support my family a little bit better," Ramirez said.
The childcare help has opened other doors for her, too.
"I'm trying to get my bachelor's. I had my son when I was 19, right when I graduated high school," Ramirez said. "It's taken me a little bit longer, but I'm getting closer to getting a degree."
A new paper from Arizona State University found that lower-income mothers in New Mexico have seen significant gains since free, universal childcare was enacted, with full-time employment increasing by 23%.
But for Lilia Doyle, in Santa Fe, working full-time won't be an option until she gets her son off a waitlist and into consistent childcare. When she first spoke to NPR in September, she said she and her family are living on her husband's income.
"Hopefully our finances will be able to absorb it," she said. "We'll buckle down, and we'll make it through, but … it's not ideal."
Then, in October, Doyle got some news: A childcare center told her they found a spot for her son – but it wouldn't open up until August 2027.
This story was supported by a reporting fellowship from the Education Writers Association.

npr.org.title: Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures
npr.org.text:
Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures
The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures.
Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years. The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years.
The results reversed a GOP dominance in legislatures that began in 2010 and had solidified since.
Going into the midterms, Republicans controlled legislatures in 28 states and Democrats held 18. The remaining few were divided. Now, with some votes still being counted, it looks likely the Democrats will hold a 24-to-22 lead with others divided.
So far, Democrats have picked up seats in nearly every state that held legislative elections, according to data compiled by NPR. Democrats gained significant ground in unexpected, reliably Republican states, like Texas, Utah and Florida.
The shift could mean real change in people's lives as legislatures rewrite laws on taxes, reproductive rights, access to health care, school funding and other issues. Legislatures have also been important in promoting or blocking President Trump's agenda.
New Democratic 'trifectas,' controlling the legislature and governor's office
The Republican State Legislative Committee, which coordinates support for GOP candidates, blamed the losses on the national anti-incumbent mood and heavy spending for Democrats. "Ultimately, the results of this cycle underscore both the challenges Republicans face and the importance of maintaining a strong, sustained presence in the states," the group's president. Edith Jorge-Tuñón, wrote.
The president of their rival organization, Heather Williams of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said their wins "proved what is possible when you put statehouses at the center of a national strategy."
Some of the biggest changes could come in states where Democrats now control both chambers of the legislature and the governor's office. They gained six new "trifectas."
In Arizona, Democrats will have the majorities in the state House and Senate and hold the governor's office — a trifecta — for the first time since 1966.
One possible policy change could be on school vouchers. Gov. Katie Hobbs has repeatedly tried to reform and limit the state's billion-dollar voucher program, which provides public money for private school tuition regardless of family income. But the Republican-run legislature had blocked her. Arizona Democrats have said they also hope to provide financial relief on rent, utilities and childcare.
In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has promised to work with a newly Democratic legislature to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, strengthen abortion rights and increase affordable housing.
Democrats also won trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and in Nevada, where they won the governor's office. They broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.
Going into the midterms, Republicans had a few more trifectas than the Democrats. Now Democrats will likely have 22 and the Republicans 17, with 10 other states divided, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. (That doesn't include Nebraska, with a Republican governor and a unicameral legislature controlled by Republicans.)
Democrats can break Republican momentum in some states
In some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, Democrats have turned Republican-controlled legislatures into divided legislatures.
Georgia Democrats won the House and came close in the Senate. On their agenda, they could try to win over a few GOP lawmakers and pass Medicaid expansion to provide health care to more low income residents. There could also be an effort by House Democrats to repeal that state's six-week abortion ban, but that could be a tough sell in the Senate.
Democrats won control the North Carolina state House. As for the state Senate, a Republican is leading the race for one seat by just over a couple hundred votes and it is likely headed to a recount. It will determine if Republicans have a one-seat majority or if the chamber will be tied. If it is tied, the Democratic lieutenant governor would be the tie-breaker.
North Carolina Democrats are expected to try and roll back some abortion restrictions. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has called on both parties to work on addressing affordability concerns once the legislature convenes.
In several states, Democrats fell short of flipping some Republican-held chambers but won enough seats to end Republican supermajorities. The Multistate government relations firm says that happened in six states that had GOP, veto-proof supermajorities.
That will matter most where there are Democratic governors, who now have leverage to veto GOP initiatives, like in North Carolina, Ohio and Kansas.
Colin Campbell of WUNC, Sarah Kallis of Georgia Public Broadcasting, Carmen Russell-Sluchansky of WHYY and Wayne Schutsky of KJZZ, contributed to this story.

npr.org.title: A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
npr.org.text:
A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
Judy Heumann is known as the mother of the disability rights movement — yet she is lesser known than many of the other civil rights activists of her time. Now, a new film seeks to change that.
Being Heumann, the latest movie from Oscar-winning director Siân Heder, tells the story of the young woman from Brooklyn who led the movement to win the first civil rights protections in the country for people with disabilities.
Before the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, there was Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. It was a single sentence, written into the law, promising people with disabilities the right to fair employment and access to public life without facing discrimination.
But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.
Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.
People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.
"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.
Regarding disability rights as basic civil rights was a novel concept at the time, but has remained core to the movement today.
Shapiro says Heumann was fueled by the idea of a generation of young disabled people who would come of age under the ADA: "They see the ADA as a floor, not a ceiling, and Judy loved that there's this new generation demanding more."
With the film having opened in theaters this month and now streaming on Apple TV, NPR sat down with some members of the ADA generation to talk about Heumann's legacy, and the threats they see today to the movement she helped launch.
"It is our job to carry on her legacy and keep that fire burning all these decades later," says Kaleigh Brendle, who started a disability rights organization called Judy's League to push back against the Trump administration's efforts to roll back protections attached to Section 504.
Last month, a federal judge dealt a blow to disability rights activists by agreeing to strip out mentions of "integration" of people with disabilities from Section 504 regulations. This erased some of the very language Heumann and her movement had helped win 50 years ago.
As she watched Being Heumann, Brendle says she "felt simultaneously sad that we're here again because I know she would be hurting to see so much of what she fought for at risk. But it also strengthened my resolve."
Brendle, who is blind and has other disabilities, held a watch party of Being Heumann with four other members of Judy's League. They spoke to NPR about their impressions.
These are excerpts from that conversation, edited for length and clarity.
On what stood out most about Being Heumann:
Liam Holland, 25, Philadelphia: The very first line of the movie is Judy chanting "[Sign 504]!" That gave me chills right away, because almost 50 years later, 504 is the exact reason we founded Judy's League. Seeing her lead the chant hit home because we are still fighting those exact same battles today.
Cricket Bidleman, 27, Baltimore: Like Liam said, seeing history come full circle was not particularly encouraging. But we did it once, so we can do it again. We can save 504.
Kaleigh Brendle, 23, Berkeley, Calif.: What I loved seeing over and over on display was just the unshakable resolve that Judy showed, that fire that would not be extinguished … And I think right now we're seeing relentless challenges to our rights from this administration, from every direction. ... It really gave me hope and renewed what I feel we need to be doing right now.
Ellana Crew, 30, Baltimore: I feel I've never seen so many real disabled people on screen in one place ... They are laughing, they are swearing, they're telling dirty jokes … That was one of my favorite things, honestly, it was just like, 'OK, wow, I didn't expect that to be in this movie.' They are not shying away from disabled people as sexual and romantic beings, which is rarely something that society lets us talk about. And ... it's remarkable how many of the sentiments in the movie, based on this time in the 1970s, still feel so relevant today.
On what parts of the disability rights movement back then still feel relevant:
Ellana Crew: A lot of attitudes expressed by non-disabled people [in the film] felt fairly indistinguishable from the attitudes I hear today. Like some of the same sentiments, some of the same opinions of pity, charity-based mindsets of like, "Oh, well we feel bad for you, but we can't do anything about it, it's just too hard." I think people would be amazed how often that still happens today, or maybe they wouldn't.
Cricket Bidleman: It's amazing to see how in some ways we've made so much progress. I mean, now we have computers and technology that work for us, and autonomous vehicles and things like that. But the discrimination hasn't really changed that much.
Kaleigh Brendle: What really moved me was hearing Judy lead the "Sign 504" chant because I, along with several other people in Judy's league ... we were in Austin, Texas on the Capitol steps this July. And all these years later we were having to chant "Hands off 504."
On how the legacy of Judy Heumann and other activists has shaped the disability rights movement today:
Liam Holland: Every week, I roll a mile and back [in my wheelchair] by myself to get chicken for my dinner puree. That trip has a lot of curb cuts. Before 504, sidewalks did not have ramps, which stopped disabled people's access to sidewalks. The [1977] sit-in forced the government to mandate public access. So every curb I go over is directly tied to that fight. ... The people at the deli see me come in every week by myself. They fist-bump me, get my card from my wallet, put it back ... And then I roll home over curb cuts listening to music. So what Judy means to me, quite simply, is independence and normalcy.
Leigh White, 30, Galloway, N.J.: Unfortunately, history rhymes. And we're not right back where we started, but we are in the crucible, if you will, where we're kind of being fired at on all sides. And it's important to remember her grit and her tenacity and her true dedication ... Disabled individuals are the largest minority group in the United States. And it crosses all genders and all races and everything. So by fighting for the rights of people with disabilities, it kind of raises all boats.
Kaleigh Brendle: I always say to other people that don't understand the disability experience: If you broke your arm tomorrow, you would expect that the world would accommodate you. You would expect to have the accommodations that you needed as you navigated that temporary disability. Why is it wrong for us to expect what you would expect in that situation?
Cricket Bidleman: We've made so many advancements because of people like Judy and because of … all these activists and advocates who came before us. And although I do have to struggle with people to obtain access to media or textbooks or the standardized testing to get into various education, it's still nothing compared to some of the things we saw in the movie
Leigh White: Us being part of the 'ADA generation,' we're able to reap the benefits. And with hindsight we're really able to appreciate the work that she's done and then kind of carry the torch into the future. So that the struggles we're going through right now, hopefully the next generation of disabled youth don't have to go through the same things.

theguardian.com.title: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
theguardian.com.text:
Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.
The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.
At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.
Weekend roundup
- Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.
- Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.
- UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.
- Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.
In depth: ‘This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms’
Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).
Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.
Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.
But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).
Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”
The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.
Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?
Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.
There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.
The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.
And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”
On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?
In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.
Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.
A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.
It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.
Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?
I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?
The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”
But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.
It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?
The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.
“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.
There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.
Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”
The week to come
- Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.
- Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.
- Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.
What else we’ve been reading
- With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture, and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team
- Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read. Poppy
- Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand’s prominence. Poppy
Sport
Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure.
Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win, with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera.
Rugby union | Tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave Scotland a 15-12 win against Australia in the Nations Championship at Murrayfield
The front pages
“PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today.
The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.
Today in Focus
Grand Theft Auto VI: the cultural event of the decade?
This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald, traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US, the setting of all its games so far.
Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron
The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.
Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”
Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday
Bored at work?
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

theguardian.com.title: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’
theguardian.com.text:
Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK, and must act quickly to increase national resilience to possibly very major crises, a parliamentary report has found.
While Labour recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, advising households to have stocks of food and water, most of the public are unaware of the scale of potential threats from cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence or strikes on underseas cables, as well as natural disasters such as extreme weather and flooding, it said.
Written by the Lords national resilience committee after months of expert hearings, the report calls for a new and coherent approach to resilience planning, including a dedicated cabinet minister and an annual statement to parliament by the prime minister to set out the extent of preparedness.
It also called for more flexible ways to communicate with the public, including a pause to plans to switch off the Freeview-style digital terrestrial TV signal, in case other systems are disrupted.
Another recommendation is for the government to send every household a booklet setting out how people can prepare for and respond to an emergency, following the model of countries such as Denmark and Sweden.
The report said the UK’s current plans were often out of date and over atomised, dealing with responses to a single emergency such as a loss of power or water supplies, or a cyber-attack, and not an increasingly plausible “polycrisis” of several disruptions blending into another, especially as AI “supercharges” the risk from cyber-attacks.
“In the face of potentially catastrophic risks and despite the recent launch of the Be Ready campaign, the government appears complacent and the UK is underprepared. We need to move fast to turn things around,” the committee warned.
“The government must not treat emerging threats as distant or hypothetical problems. Doing so risks leaving the UK exposed as vulnerabilities develop.”
Among the particular vulnerabilities highlighted are medicines and food, both of which are dependent on highly centralised and generally international supply chains, with few if any back-up options if these are disrupted.
The bulk of antibiotic medicines are now made in China or India, the report noted, with about 90% of the world’s 6-APA, the organic compound which is the basis of penicillin-types antibiotics, coming from China.
This is, it said, the result of years of price pressures and cost-based procurement, meaning there is now only one integrated penicillin facility in Europe, and none in the UK.
The same is true for other medical supplies, with one witness telling the committee that such was the reliance on overseas-made items such as scissors and medical staplers that disrupted could badly disrupt many everyday surgical operations.
With food, the committee was told that while people stockpiling several days of food and water, as recommended by Be Ready, was something, this did not cover the wider strategic risks to a hugely centralised food system.
This results in almost 95% of UK retail food being supplied by just nine companies from 131 distribution hubs, meaning that disruption to just a handful of firms could create very significant disruption.
Despite the increasing risk of multi-area crises, too much current emergency planning remains “organised in silos around individual risks, organisations and sectors, rather than the continued operation of essential national functions”, the report said, calling for this to change.
There was, it set out, a particular risk to digital communications, including through possible attacks on undersea cables. BT, which has a dominant role in this area, has access to just two cable repair ships, the report found – “one French-owned and generally unavailable, and one UK-based but 35 years old”.
Among its recommendations, the report said the Cabinet Office, which leads on resilience, should set out a national resilience strategy within six months, with proper funding and a more coherent assessment than the current national risk register, which lists 87 separate items.
It also called for resilience to be embedded in civilian life, with a national register of volunteers and civil reservists drawn up, and the possibility of an entitlement to paid leave for people taking resilience-based training.
Jean Coussins, the cross-bench peer who chairs the committee, said ministers should not be “squeamish” about setting out the risks.
She said: “Evidence shows that the public would be reassured, not alarmed, by candid information. People are more than willing to step up in an emergency, but less clear [as to] why and how.”
A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office said it would “carefully review” the specific recommendations, but that the government was already working at speed.
“From launching a national campaign to raise awareness of the simple steps households can take to stay safe in everyday emergencies, to delivering the largest home defence exercise in recent history next year, and investing over £1bn in pandemic security – our work on resilience goes further than successive governments have ever gone before.
“However, we know there is still more work to do to make the UK the most resilient country we can be, including working with and learning from our allies.”

theguardian.com.title: Home Office accused of trying to cancel online talk by Andreas Malm
theguardian.com.text:
Shabana Mahmood has been accused of an “assault” on free speech over claims her officials tried to cancel an online talk by the climate academic Andreas Malm days after he was banned from entering the UK.
The event in Hackney, east London, was a launch party for the socialist magazine Tribune. It went ahead on 4 November in defiance of Home Office warnings.
While the Home Office has denied it tried to cancel the event, its officials warned Hackney council, which owns the venue, that the event could breach counter-terrorism laws because it was also due to be addressed by the Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori. The event took place on the day she was challenging the group’s proscription in the supreme court.
Hackney’s Green party mayor, Zoe Garbett, who intervened to ensure the event went ahead, has accused Mahmood of an “appalling assault on free speech” and written to her demanding an explanation.
Days before the event, Malm, a respected climate academic and author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, was prevented from travelling to the UK. Officials told him that his presence was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”, but no further reasons were given.
Documents released to Tribune under freedom of information laws detail how Hackney council officials appeared to have been pressed by the Home Office to cancel the event, despite the department’s own assessment that it was “unlikely to meet the threshold for disruption”.
An email on 12 October from the Home Office’s extremism disruptions team said: “We received this referral from the counter-extremism group (CEG) about [Malm] due to visit the UK for an event in London on 4 November.
“[Malm] has made many statements in support of terrorists and direct action, particularly regarding Palestine and climate change.”
After Malm was prevented from entering the UK, in a decision that was widely criticised, Tribune said he would still speak at the event via a video link. A day before the event, a Home Office official emailed Hackney council’s Prevent and hate-crime coordinator to describe Malm and Ammori as “two speakers of concern”.
An official from the Home Office’s Prevent local delivery unit also told the council: “Ultimately, I can’t direct you to cancel the event. This is a decision for the council.”
But they went on to warn that the event could breach the Terrorism Act 2000 “whereby it is an offence if a person … assists in arranging … a meeting which he knows is to be addressed by a person who belongs … to a proscribed organisation”.
Mahmood’s officials also asked Hackney if managers of the venue had been told of their concerns about Malm and Ammori speaking at the event “even if it is to take place virtually”.
After those concerns were passed on, a manager at the venue called Tribune to say the event would have to be cancelled, according to its editor, Oliver Eagleton. This decision was then overruled by the mayor.
In her letter to the home secretary, Garbett said: “Encouraging the cancellation of lawful public events represents an assault on the right to free speech and under no circumstance will I be complicit in it.”
She added: “Despite initial Home Office assessments indicating that the event was ‘unlikely to meet the threshold for disruption’, pressure was applied to council staff to intervene with the operator and cancel the booking.”
The letter asked: “Why was pressure exerted on local council officers to consider cancelling or vetoing speakers, and how does the Home Office reconcile these actions with local authorities’ statutory obligations to uphold free speech and peaceful assembly.”
A Home Office spokesperson said it was “categorically untrue to suggest the Home Office pushed for this event to be cancelled”, pointing out it was a decision for the council, informed by Home Office advice.
Malm said: “The UK’s crackdown on free expression is terrifying. First they ban the books of Sally Rooney. Then they block people like me from entering the country because of our support for Palestine. Now it comes to light that they tried to cancel this magazine launch – just because they feared that the speakers might say something they disagree with. Where will this repression end?”
Ammori said: “By trying to prevent me from being able to speak publicly, the Home Office has further proven the case I was making in the supreme court that same day about the authorities misapplying the law to carry out unlawful arrests and unlawful acts of censorship such as this.
“Home Office officials wrongly advised the council that this entirely lawful political discussion would breach the Terrorism Act simply because I was due to participate. I have never been convicted of any crime, let alone a terrorism offence, but people convicted under the Terrorism Act are not gagged as a result and barred from speaking publicly. The suggestion that my participation in a political discussion could somehow make that discussion unlawful is ludicrous.”

theguardian.com.title: Weakening UK electric vehicle targets would hurt car industry, ministers told
theguardian.com.text:
Moves to weaken the UK’s targets on electric vehicles would hurt the car industry as well as consumers, campaigners and experts have said before a key intervention from government advisers expected this week.
The climate change committee (CCC) will write to ministers on Wednesday about the effects of changing the zero emissions vehicle (ZEV) mandate on the cost of living and the UK’s net zero targets.
The current mandate stipulates that 80% of new car sales will have to be electric from 2030, and 100% from 2035, but it has been reported that Labour is poised to reduce those targets.
Campaigners said the evidence to be examined by the CCC all pointed to consumers losing out from any weakening of the targets.
The CCC has kept its deliberations under wraps, but its chair, Nigel Topping, has a long history of advocacy for electric vehicles. He was involved in the automotive sector in various roles for two decades, and has frequently urged carmakers to move faster to electric vehicles, which are more efficient and cheaper to run than their fossil-fuelled counterparts while producing less air pollution and carbon dioxide.
He has also long been a champion of UK innovation and engineering, and believes the UK’s target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 is spurring economic growth and creating jobs. He has said: “Our leadership in decarbonisation is driving industrial leadership, which is driving competitiveness and growth.”
If the CCC letter is critical of proposals to weaken the ZEV mandate, ministers will face an uphill task to justify such a decision. Doing so would hamper efforts to reduce the cost of living, because it would slow the market for electric cars, which are much cheaper to run, analysts and campaigners say. Filling up a petrol-fuelled car can currently cost more than £100, while an electric vehicle can be fully charged for less than £10.
The head of politics at Greenpeace UK, Ami McCarthy, said: “Watering down the current sales targets for EVs would be like driving with the handbrake on. The UK has an upbeat story to tell on electrification but the car industry keeps trying to drag it backwards.
“The prime minister was absolutely right in his speech [to the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday] when he said we need industry to play their part. Aligning our sales targets with the EU would only slow us down.”
Carmakers say the UK’s current targets are too onerous and that they are having to heavily discount vehicles in order to sell enough to meet them. The chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, Mike Hawes, said manufacturers were investing billions in ZEV but that demand remained below the targets.
“Regulation mustn’t undermine UK competitiveness or hold back the transition,” he said. “Government must act now, with fundamental change to the targets, backed by ongoing and increased support for consumers, including incentives, affordable charging, and tackling disincentives.”.”
One expert, however, pointed out that the UK was exceeding its current sales target by a significant margin, whereas if manufacturers were struggling, the target would be barely met. “That shows it’s nonsense to say they’re discounting heavily,” they said. “EVs are so clearly the future, it is hard to understand why the car industry is not embracing them.”
Most of the UK’s cars are sold for export, and sales of EVs are growing strongly in the EU, a major market for manufacturers. Given that Chinese competitors face EU tariffs, the UK could seize an advantage over its rivals if it pushed harder for EVs, the analyst said. Sales of battery-only electric vehicles rose by half last month compared with the same month last year.
McCarthy said sales in the UK were strong and benefitting households. “It’s great to see minister Katie White celebrating the fact that an electric vehicle is sold every 52 seconds in the UK,” they said.
“While the EU seems to be dropping into second gear, the UK has an opportunity to ensure British companies and consumers reap the rewards. Leading from the front isn’t just good for UK industry. It will help lower the cost of living, increase energy security and reach our climate goals.”
A government spokesperson said: “We remain committed to the phase out of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets.
“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

theguardian.com.title: Special needs overhaul in England could bring in new avenues for extra support
theguardian.com.text:
Families of children with special needs may get new avenues to appeal for extra support at school, under major concessions being considered for the government’s overhaul of special needs education in England.
The move comes as the government’s reforms are being repeatedly criticised by campaigners and parents’ groups for watering down legal protections allowing families to appeal through a high court tribunal for support.
Lucy Powell, the education secretary, has told MPs who raised the issue to “wait and see”, hinting that changes to the appeals process were “a key part of what we are looking at to make sure there are those mechanisms in place”.
Stakeholders involved in the discussions told the Guardian that two independent appeal routes were under consideration, allowing families a forum to complain if they are dissatisfied with the provision offered by their child’s school.
The government’s white paper on special education needs and disability (Send) provision and funding, published in February, replaces the widespread use of agreements known as education, health and care plans (EHCPs) with new tiers of support to be managed by schools, known as individual support plans (ISPs).
But while parents can currently appeal to an independent first-tier Send tribunal to resolve disputes over EHCPs, the government’s reforms would restrict that route and instead see complaints over ISPs dealt with by each child’s school – which special needs groups quickly criticised as inadequate.
In response, policymakers began considering new appeal routes after the white paper was published under Bridget Phillipson as education secretary.
One route would allow parents to appeal to the local government and social care ombudsman, which already investigates complaints made against local authorities over Send provision and school transport.
An alternative route could be parents appealing to an independent review panel, modelled on the panels that hear appeals against school exclusions. These panels have the power to overturn exclusion decisions, and are appointed by local authorities with a clerk and up to five experts who have no direct connection to the school involved.
Jane Harris, the chief executive of Speech and Language UK, a charity, said: “Children with speech and language challenges and their families have been let down for far too long.
“So any new appeals system must give parents a genuinely independent, swift and effective way to challenge decisions and secure the education and therapy their children need to thrive.
“Schools and nurseries cannot be expected to mark their own homework, however. Leaving them with the final say would not only undermine parents’ confidence in the system but also risk damaging relationships between families and the very people responsible for supporting their children every day.
“Whatever body hears appeals, the people hearing them must be independent and have the right expertise, and their decisions must be legally meaningful and lead to timely action. Anything else leaves children at risk.”
Madeleine Cassidy, the chief executive of Ipsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said it was “encouraging” that the government was considering alternatives.
Cassidy said: “The proposal to weaken the powers of the Send tribunal and reduce families’ opportunities to challenge decisions has been a significant source of concern for parents and carers of children and young people with Send.
“Ipsea has long called for the local government and social care ombudsman’s remit to be extended to schools so that complaints about the support children with Send receive can be independently investigated.
“However, stronger complaints mechanisms must not come at the expense of robust, enforceable legal rights.”
A Department for Education spokesperson said: “We know parents want reassurance their child will get the support they need, and that they have clear routes to resolution if things do go wrong.
“We are considering all the input we have received from our engagement events and consultation and it would not be right to get ahead of that.
“In the meantime, we’re investing in schools to improve inclusion and build a system where every child gets the right support, in their local area, without a fight.”
Powell was questioned this month by parliament’s education select committee, with Mark Sewards, the Labour MP for Leeds South West and Morley, telling her that parents were concerned about losing rights of appeal.
Powell replied: “This is a complex area. We are absolutely determined in these closing stages to get that detail right so families and parents do feel, yes, there’s a level playing field, but also there’s accountability in the system.”
The government’s bill and its response to its consultation on the Send white paper is not expected to be ready until early next year.
But the latest official statistics underline the importance of the appeals processes and the urgent need for reform.
In October, the government revealed that the average waiting time for a final oral hearing at the Send tribunal is longer than 18 months, meaning that an appeal lodged now would wait until May 2028 to be heard.
The tribunal is also receiving record numbers of appeals, with 8,800 lodged with the high court in the three months to June alone. The tribunal’s backlog rose to 18,000 appeals, a 31% increase since 2025.

theguardian.com.title: MP Helen Haines’s first words since leaving hospital after alleged attack led to double amputation
theguardian.com.text:
The independent Australian MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked by a man outside her electorate office in Victoria resulting in the amputation of both her legs.
In a statement, Haines said she had moved to the rehabilitation stage of her recovery, which would continue in Melbourne.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred [hospital] and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing.”
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said his thoughts were with Haines.
“We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese said in a statement.
Haines said she was “overwhelmed” by the many Australians who had donated to the Save the Children charity fundraiser.
Her husband, Phil Haines, had made the request to the public on her behalf to donate to the charity in lieu of flowers in the aftermath of the alleged attack.
As of Monday afternoon, more than $1.46m had been raised for the charity through Haines’s fundraising appeal.
“I am overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians in the form of donations to Save the Children and I look forward to working with them in due course on applying these funds to improve the lives of children.”
Haines, the federal member for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was repeatedly struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta on 19 October. Her condition was then downgraded to “serious but stable” on 24 October.
Police will allege the 65-year-old was standing by the boot of her car outside her electoral office when a car did a U-turn and struck her repeatedly.
Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated. He is known to her family.
Police charged Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
Police have also charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.
The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, paid tribute to Haines in the Senate on Monday and on behalf of the parliament wished her strength through her challenging rehabilitation.
“It says a great deal about her character that even as she faces these challenges, in her statement she looks ahead to the work she wants to do to improve the lives of children following the donations to Save the Children that Australians made at her request. It is an example of her determination and her generosity that is so admired,” Wong said.
The leader of the opposition in the Senate, Michaelia Cash, added that Haines’s discharge from hospital was warmly welcomed across the parliament.
“She has demonstrated extraordinary courage and resilience. And on behalf, in particular, of my Coalition Senate colleagues, we wish Helen every strength during her continued recovery.”
Haines has been given leave of absence until 26 November, the last sitting day of the year.
MPs across parliament have expressed concern for their safety and that of their staff since the alleged attack, and prompted conversations about the temperature of political debate.
Albanese, during the last parliamentary sitting, warned against the rise in anger “that distorts and corrodes our public discourse”, and urged voters and politicians not to ignore it.
“Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but towards workers in hospitality and retail, in schools and in hospitals, towards police, paramedics, and other officials, we are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence.”
The independent MP Allegra Spender said it was “wonderful” news that Haines was making good progress in her recovery.
“She is a remarkable person and her strength and positivity after everything that has happened inspires me.”

theguardian.com.title: Ministers accused of ‘gambling with safety’ for not knowing cost of NHS maternity unit repairs
theguardian.com.text:
Ministers have been accused of “gambling with the safety of mothers and babies” after admitting they do not know how much repairing decrepit maternity units would cost.
NHS chiefs said last year that shoddy infrastructure meant 43% of maternity and neonatal units in England did not meet basic safety standards. Infrastructure problems hampered the delivery of clinical care thousands of times every year, NHS England said.
The Care Quality Commission (CQC) watchdog has also voiced concern that lack of space, ageing facilities and shortage of operating theatres presents “serious safety risks” for mothers and babies.
The latest warning over risks to women’s safety has been made by the Liberal Democrats amid growing concern that leaks, broken equipment and cramped treatment areas are disrupting the delivery of maternity care.
However, Karin Smyth, the NHS minister at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), admitted in responses to recent parliamentary questions that it could not put a figure on how much it would cost to upgrade maternity and neonatal units that NHS England believed either needed significant repair or replacement soon or were running “a serious risk of imminent breakdown”.
Smyth made the admission in response to questions tabled by Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson.
“NHS England has spelt out in black and white just how serious this is, with dozens of maternity units falling apart and some at serious risk of imminent breakdown,” said Morgan.
“It is appalling that, despite those warnings, the government still has no idea how much it would cost to make every maternity unit fit for purpose. Ministers are gambling with the safety of mothers, babies and NHS staff caring for them.”
The maternity unit at Musgrove Park hospital in Taunton, Somerset, is “old and not designed to deliver 21st-century care”, Baroness Valerie Amos’s review of childbirth services concluded in the summer. She found “leaking roofs, poor temperature control with rooms often too hot or too cold”.
The unit’s antenatal ward is in such a state of disrepair that it is being propped up by metal poles.
Musgrove Park bosses acknowledged in September that its maternity unit is “old, outdated and cramped” after CQC inspectors found that water had leaked into clinical areas and mould had formed on the walls and ceilings of the postnatal ward, although they rated the care staff provided as good.
Last week, Jules Wilkinson described how he had to hold up a light that had come loose from the ceiling for an hour while his wife was giving birth to their daughter Cora in the maternity unit at Stepping Hill hospital in Stockport, Greater Manchester. The light narrowly missed a midwife as it came off the ceiling.
So much of the 121-year-old hospital is falling apart that “it’s almost in a death spiral”, Wilkinson added. Stepping Hill, which regularly suffers leaks, needs £400m to ensure it is safe for patients and staff, its chief executive, Karen James, believes.
“There is a clear link between the condition of service infrastructure, the experience of service users and staff, and safety,” NHS England’s review of the infrastructure of maternity and neonatal units, published in September 2025, concluded.
“In the last three years there have been 14,519 formally reported instances in the maternity and neonatal estate where clinical services have been interrupted or service delivery has been impacted as a direct result of poor physical conditions.”
Problems such as power outages and faulty nurse call systems put “additional pressure on already stretched staff … and can lead directly to procedures delays, such as planned caesarean sections”, it added.
In 2024, the CQC warned in a report that “too many maternity units are currently not fit for purpose, lacking space, facilities and, in a small number of cases, the appropriate levels of potentially life-saving equipment. We are concerned about the serious safety risks this presents for women and babies.”
St Helier hospital in Sutton, south London, is being forced to relocate its maternity services because of urgently needed repairs.
The “significant [repair] work” planned cannot be done “while maintaining a good birth, gynaecology and fertility experience and safe environment for babies and families in the building”, said Mat Shaw, the chief executive of the NHS trust that runs St Helier.
In last month’s budget, ministers cut £1bn from on the NHS’s capital budget over the next four years, to help boost defence spending.
The cut is despite the fact that the cost of eradicating the NHS’s massive backlog of maintenance has risen to £17.3bn, according to the most recent official figures.
Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of the NHS Alliance, said: “A lot of maternity units are located in outdated, decaying buildings, making it much harder to ensure safe, high-quality care. This comes on top of wider challenges including staffing, the size and location of some units and the increasing complexity of care.”
The DHSC blamed the Conservatives’ failure to properly maintain the physical fabric of the NHS during their time in office for the poor state of so many childbirth units.
“This government inherited struggling maternity services in buildings left to crumble,” a spokesperson said.
“That is why we’ve invested £271m since April 2025 into schemes related to critical safety risks in the maternity and neonatal estate and recently announced more than £1.5bn to improve NHS buildings and facilities.
“We know there is a long way to go, but we have backed the NHS with a record capital budget for health, rising to £15bn in 2029-30. Our 10-year capital plan will also put investment on a long-term footing and rebuild the health service for mothers, babies and all the other patients who rely on it.”

theguardian.com.title: Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government?
theguardian.com.text: Spaniards head to the polls on 29 November to vote in the country’s sixth general election in 11 years. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government for the first time since Spain’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Franco.

theguardian.com.title: Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
theguardian.com.text:
The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”
He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.
“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”
The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.
Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”
Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.
The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.
Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.
Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

theguardian.com.title: Coles investigates cyber-attack and apologises to customers
theguardian.com.text:
Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised.
Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts.
“Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange.
“We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems.
“Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.”
Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”.
“We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said.
“We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.”
Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they received unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links.
In a separate and unrelated incident, Woolworths said it was aware of reports from customers who purchased compromised e-gift cards. The ABC first reported on Monday some customers had lost hundreds of dollars after buying the company’s Everyday WISH gift cards through its rewards website or app, only to find the sums loaded on to them had been spent by someone else.
Some customers told the national broadcaster they had lost up to $500, with transactions showing up at stores in different states to where they purchased the cards.
“We are aware of reports of an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and are looking into the matter as a priority,” a Woolworths spokesperson said in a statement. “We recognise the concern this has caused affected customers and we apologise to customers impacted. We encourage any customer who notices a transaction they don’t recognise to contact our Gift Card Support team.”
The company says it is working through all reported issues and will look into replacing affected e-gift cards.
– Additional reporting by Nick Visser

theguardian.com.title: Tech failure forces hundreds of University of Melbourne students to abandon final exams mid-test
theguardian.com.text:
Hundreds of students at the University of Melbourne were forced to abandon their final exams on Monday morning after many were unable to access the digital platform needed to begin them.
Jol Scobie, a first-year student at the university, was set to take his Australian politics exam on Monday after preparing for weeks. He had initially been told earlier in the year it was going to be a hand-written essay before instructors changed the test to a digital platform.
The subject was one of several holding exams at the Royal Exhibition Building in Carlton, with hundreds of students in attendance on Monday. About half were able to log on to the digital system and begin, Scobie said, but many others were left sitting at their desks, staring at a blank screen for about 50 minutes.
Students undertaking the Australian politics exam were meant to complete two 1,000-word essays over two hours.
“The [exam coordinators] said: ‘Listen, we can’t get it to work. It’s time for everyone to leave,’” Scobie said. “We were sort of standing there watching hundreds and hundreds of students pour out of the building.”
A university spokesperson confirmed technical issues caused the cancellation of a “small number” of exams on both 11 and 16 November.
“Early indications are that the issue relates to third-party technical partners involved in the delivery of our digital exams,” the spokesperson said. “Our teams are following established contingency processes to resolve the issue and communicate alternative arrangements for the students affected.
“We understand exam disruptions can be stressful for our students, and have support services available to assist students as needed.”
The university did not immediately reply to questions about how many students were affected, and if they would be able to sit makeup examinations before Friday.
Millie Mountford, another first-year student, said there had been limited communication about when a makeup exam would be held and when students and the university would be able to fit them in during an already busy week. Thousands of other students will be sitting their own tests in the coming days, with Mountford herself having another scheduled for tomorrow.
She does not know if it will go forward without any issues.
“I’m just kind of demotivated to study when I don’t even know if it will actually be worth it,” she said. “It’s just majorly inconvenient.”
Charlotte Wickham said the cancelled exam could snarl her travel plans to see her family in Tasmania over the holiday break due to the high cost and limited ability to change flights at the last minute.
“The stress really comes from not knowing if they are going to reschedule [the exams for] the supplementary period,” she said. “We have these questions that we’ve specifically studied for and now we have such a long period of waiting. We’ve planned our lives, and we have to keep these at the back of our minds. Do we have to restudy because the questions are different?”
The issues come after the National Tertiary Education Union organised a 24-hour strike and four-day teaching ban in October amid concerns from members about academic workloads, AI protections and fair pay. Members voted to approve a proposed new enterprise agreement to address some of those concerns earlier in November.
Last week, the Age reported the University of Melbourne was planning to cut almost 180 jobs across mainly non-academic staff after “disappointing” financial results.

theguardian.com.title: Queensland and NT to stick with puberty blocker bans for transgender children against NHMRC advice
theguardian.com.text:
